Measurement, Units and Vectors
A number without a unit is nothing

Physics is the art of measuring the world and finding patterns in the numbers. But a number alone means little. Is 5 a distance, a time, a price? In 1999 NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter was lost near Mars. One team's software gave thrust in pound-force seconds; another team's expected newton seconds. The spacecraft passed too close and was destroyed. A unit mix-up cost a whole mission. So we begin with the grammar of physics: units, dimensions, errors and vectors. Everything later in the course is built on them.
The SI system: one language for everyone

Scientists worldwide use the SI (Systeme International). It has seven base units: metre (length) kilogram (mass) second (time) ampere (electric current) kelvin (temperature) mole (amount of substance) candela (light intensity) All other units are built from these. A newton, for example, is kg m/s squared. Since 2019 the base units are fixed by nature's constants, not by a metal block. The metre is the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second.
Dimensions: a free error detector

Every quantity has a dimension : length (L), mass (M), time (T). Speed is L/T. Acceleration is L/T squared. Force is M L/T squared. The rule: you can only add or equate quantities with the same dimensions. You cannot add 3 metres to 2 seconds. This gives a quick test. Suppose you half-remember that distance = speed x time squared. Dimensions: L on the left, (L/T) x T squared = L x T on the right. They do not match, so the formula is wrong. Dimensional checking cannot prove a formula right, but it catches many wrong ones in seconds.
Every measurement has an error

No instrument is perfect. A ruler marked in millimetres cannot give you a length better than about half a millimetre. We report this as significant figures : 2.5 cm means we trust two digits; 2.50 cm claims more care. When you multiply or divide, the answer should have no more significant figures than the least precise input. If a plate is 2.5 m by 1.25 m, its area is 3.1 square metres, not 3.125. Honest numbers carry their uncertainty. This habit is what separates a scientist from a salesperson.
Scalars and vectors

Some quantities need only a size: mass, time, temperature, energy. These are scalars . Others need a size and a direction: displacement, velocity, force. These are vectors . Saying 'walk 5 km' is not enough; you must say which way. We draw a vector as an arrow. Length shows size; the arrowhead shows direction. To add vectors, place them head to tail. The arrow from the first tail to the last head is the sum, called the resultant .
Components: breaking an arrow into two

Any vector in a plane can be split into two perpendicular parts, left-right (x) and up-down (y). For a vector of size V at angle theta from the x-axis: Components Vx = V cos(theta) Vy = V sin(theta) V = square root of (Vx squared + Vy squared) To add vectors, add their x parts and their y parts separately. This turns a messy geometry problem into simple arithmetic, and it is the trick physicists use all through mechanics and electricity.
Walk 3 km east, then 4 km north

Distance travelled is a scalar: 3 + 4 = 7 km. Displacement is a vector. The x part is 3 km, the y part is 4 km. Size = square root of (9 + 16) = square root of 25 = 5 km . Direction: tan(theta) = 4/3, so theta is about 53 degrees north of east. You walked 7 km but ended only 5 km from the start. Distance and displacement are different things. If you walk a full circle and return home, your distance is large but your displacement is zero.
Common mix-ups

Mass is not weight. Mass (kg) is how much matter you have. Weight is a force (newtons) that depends on gravity. Your mass is the same on the Moon; your weight is about one-sixth. Vectors do not add like plain numbers. 3 N plus 4 N can be 7 N, 5 N or 1 N, depending on direction. More digits does not mean more accuracy. A calculator shows eight digits; your ruler gave you two.
Who keeps India's measures?

India adopted the metric system by law in the 1950s through the Standards of Weights and Measures Act, 1956, replacing seers, maunds and miles. The CSIR-National Physical Laboratory in New Delhi is the custodian of India's national standards. It maintains atomic clocks that realise Indian Standard Time, and the accuracy of every shop scale ultimately traces back to such standards. India also uses SI units in its space missions. ISRO's engineers work in newtons, kilograms and seconds, so a Mars Climate Orbiter-style error would be just as fatal for them.
Key takeaways

Every physical quantity has a number and a unit. Mixing units is a real danger. SI has seven base units; others are combinations. Dimensions let you check formulas quickly. Scalars have size; vectors have size and direction. Split vectors into x and y components, add each separately. Think about it 1. Why can a runner who finishes a lap on a circular track have a large distance but zero displacement? 2. A formula says energy = mass x speed. Without knowing physics, how could you test it?
Motion in a Line and in a Plane
Describing motion without asking why

Before asking what makes things move, physics first learns to describe motion exactly. A cricket ball leaves the bat, rises, slows, turns and falls. Where is it? How fast? When does it land? The branch that answers this is kinematics . Its tools are simple: position, velocity, acceleration and a few equations. Once you own them, you can predict where a ball, a car or a rocket will be, using nothing but arithmetic.
Velocity: how quickly position changes

Speed is how fast; velocity is speed with direction. Average velocity is displacement divided by time: Average velocity v = change in position / change in time If a train covers 120 km in 2 hours, its average speed is 60 km/h. But the speedometer shows instantaneous speed, the speed at one moment. On a graph of position against time, instantaneous velocity is the slope of the line at that point.
Acceleration: how quickly velocity changes

Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes: Acceleration a = change in velocity / time A car going from 0 to 20 m/s in 5 s has a = 20/5 = 4 m/s squared. Every second, its speed grows by 4 m/s. Braking is also acceleration (negative, or deceleration). So is turning a corner at steady speed, because the direction of velocity is changing. Anything that changes velocity, in size or direction, is accelerating.
Three equations for steady acceleration

When acceleration a is constant, starting speed u, final speed v, time t, distance s: Equations of motion v = u + a t s = u t + (1/2) a t squared v squared = u squared + 2 a s On a speed-time graph the slope is the acceleration and the area under the line is the distance travelled. The equations are just this geometry written in algebra.
Free fall: gravity's steady pull

Near Earth's surface, anything falling freely gains about 9.8 m/s of speed every second. We call this g = 9.8 m/s squared. Galileo (around 1600) argued that heavy and light bodies fall together; air resistance is what makes a feather lag. In 1971 on the Moon, where there is no air, astronaut David Scott of Apollo 15 dropped a hammer and a feather together. They landed at the same instant. Gravity on the Moon is about one-sixth of Earth's, but the lesson is the same: in free fall, mass does not matter.
Projectiles: two motions at once

Throw a ball at an angle. Its motion splits into two independent parts: Horizontal: no force, so constant speed. Vertical: gravity pulls, so constant acceleration downwards. Combine them and you get a curve called a parabola. For launch speed u at angle theta (level ground), the range is R = u squared x sin(2 theta) / g. This is largest at 45 degrees. Two angles that add to 90 degrees, such as 30 and 60, give the same range.
Ball thrown straight up at 20 m/s

Take g = 9.8 m/s squared. At the top the speed is zero, so v squared = u squared - 2 g h gives: 0 = 400 - 19.6 h, so h = 20.4 m . Time to the top: v = u - g t gives 0 = 20 - 9.8 t, so t = 2.04 s. Coming down takes the same, so total flight is about 4.1 s . It returns to your hand at 20 m/s, the same speed it left with, but pointing down.
Where intuition slips

'At the top the ball has no acceleration.' Wrong. Its velocity is momentarily zero but gravity still pulls: a = 9.8 m/s squared downward all the time. 'Heavier things fall faster.' Only because of air. In a vacuum all fall together. 'The ball keeps going because of a force from the bat.' After release the only force is gravity (and a little air drag).
Launching east from Sriharikota

ISRO launches most satellites eastwards from Sriharikota (about 13.7 degrees north). The Earth spins eastwards, giving the launch pad a free speed of roughly 450 m/s, so the rocket needs less fuel to reach orbital speed. This is the same idea as adding velocities in vectors. On the sports field, Neeraj Chopra won javelin gold at the Tokyo Olympics with a throw of 87.58 m. A javelin is a projectile, but it is also a glider, so the best angle is not exactly 45 degrees.
Key takeaways

Velocity is the rate of change of position; acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. For steady acceleration: v = u + at, s = ut + (1/2)at squared, v squared = u squared + 2as. In free fall everything accelerates at g = 9.8 m/s squared, regardless of mass. A projectile's horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Think about it 1. A ball thrown up passes you at the same height going up and down. How do the two speeds compare? 2. Why can a car going round a bend at steady 60 km/h still be accelerating?
Newton's Laws of Motion
Why does anything move at all?

For about 2000 years people believed, following Aristotle, that a moving object needs a continuing push. It seems obvious: stop pushing a cart and it stops. Galileo and then Isaac Newton overturned this. In his Principia (1687), Newton set out three laws that explain the motion of falling apples, rolling carts, planets and rockets. They remain the working rules of engineering today.
First law: things keep doing what they are doing

An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion keeps moving in a straight line at steady speed, unless a net force acts on it . This tendency is called inertia . The cart stops not because motion needs a push, but because friction pushes back. On ice, with little friction, a puck slides far. In space, with none, it would slide forever. Inertia explains why you lurch forward when a bus brakes: your body wants to keep moving.
Second law: force makes acceleration

Newton's second law F = m a Net force F (in newtons) equals mass m (kg) times acceleration a (m/s squared). One newton is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s squared. Two lessons. First, the same push gives a light object more acceleration than a heavy one. Second, net matters: if you push a wall and it does not move, other forces (the wall's push back) balance yours, so the net force is zero.
Third law: forces come in pairs

When body A pushes on body B, B pushes back on A with an equal and opposite force. Swimming: you push water backward, water pushes you forward. A rocket throws hot gas down; the gas pushes the rocket up. It needs no air to push against, which is why rockets work in space. The key point: the two forces act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other when you work out the motion of one body.
Free-body diagrams and friction

To solve any problem, draw one object and every force on it. This is a free-body diagram . Friction opposes sliding. A good model: f = mu x N, where N is the normal force (the table's push) and mu is the friction coefficient. Rubber on dry road might have mu near 0.8; ice, near 0.05.
Weight, mass and the normal force

Mass (kg) is how much matter a body has. Weight is the gravitational force on it: W = m g. A 10 kg box weighs 10 x 9.8 = 98 N on Earth. When a box sits on a table, the table pushes up with a normal force N (normal means at right angles to the surface). Here N equals the weight, so the net vertical force is zero and the box does not accelerate. In a lift accelerating upward, N becomes bigger than your weight, and you feel heavier. That 'feeling of weight' is really the normal force.
Pushing a 10 kg box

You push with 50 N. Friction is 20 N backwards. Vertical forces (weight and normal) cancel. Net force = 50 - 20 = 30 N. F = m a gives a = 30/10 = 3 m/s squared . After 4 s from rest its speed is 12 m/s, and it has covered (1/2) x 3 x 16 = 24 m. Weight of the box: 10 x 9.8 = 98 N, so N = 98 N, and with mu = 20/98 about 0.2 for that friction.
Three classic errors

'Motion needs a force.' No. Changing motion needs a force. Steady motion needs none. 'Action and reaction cancel, so nothing can move.' They act on different bodies, so each body can still accelerate. 'Heavy objects have more inertia only on Earth.' Inertia is mass; it is the same in space. An astronaut is just as hard to push around on the Space Station.
From Sriharikota to the Moon's south pole

Every ISRO launch, from the PSLV to the LVM3 rocket that carried Chandrayaan-3, is Newton's third law at work: hot gas goes down, the rocket goes up. Chandrayaan-3's lander Vikram touched down near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023, making India the fourth country to soft-land on the Moon. Every burn that slowed it was a calculation of F = ma, with thrust and mass changing as fuel was used.
Key takeaways

Objects keep their velocity unless a net force acts (inertia). F = ma: net force gives acceleration, in newtons for kg and m/s squared. Forces come in equal, opposite pairs on different bodies. Draw a free-body diagram and add forces as vectors. Think about it 1. Why does a coin on a card fall into the glass when you flick the card away quickly? 2. A truck and a small car collide. Which feels the larger force, and which the larger acceleration?
Work, Energy and Power
The universe's most useful bank account

Energy is the one quantity physicists trust above all. It can change form, from a falling stone's motion to heat, from sunlight to electricity, but the total never changes. That rule lets you solve problems that Newton's laws would make painful. You do not need to track every force along a roller coaster; you only need to know where it starts and ends.
Work: force over distance

In physics, work is done when a force moves something. Work W = F x d x cos(theta) Here theta is the angle between force and motion. The unit is the joule (J): one newton pushing through one metre. Holding a heavy bag still does no work in this sense, since nothing moves. Carrying it level also does no work on the bag, because your upward force is at right angles to the motion (cos 90 = 0). Lifting it does work.
Kinetic energy: the energy of motion

Kinetic energy KE = (1/2) m v squared Note the square. Double your speed and the energy goes up four times. That is why a car crash at 100 km/h is far worse than at 50 km/h, and why stopping distances grow so fast. The work-energy theorem : the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.
Potential energy: stored energy

Lift a mass m to height h and you store energy in the gravitational field: Gravitational PE PE = m g h Stretch a spring, compress a gas, separate two charges: all store potential energy. Release it and it turns back into motion. A force like gravity, where the work done depends only on start and end points, is called conservative .
Conservation of energy

If only conservative forces act, KE + PE stays constant. A ball rolling down a hill trades height for speed. With friction, mechanical energy appears to vanish, but it has turned into heat. Count the heat and the total is still the same. This is the law of conservation of energy .
Power: how fast energy flows

Power P = W / t Power is work done per second. The unit is the watt : one joule per second. A 100 W bulb uses 100 J every second. One horsepower is about 746 W. Your electricity bill counts in kilowatt-hours (kWh). One kWh is 1000 W for 3600 s, which is 3.6 million joules. That is one 'unit' of electricity.
A 2 kg stone dropped from 5 m

PE at the top: m g h = 2 x 9.8 x 5 = 98 J . Just before landing all of it is KE: (1/2) x 2 x v squared = 98, so v squared = 98 and v is about 9.9 m/s . Notice the mass cancels: v = square root of (2 g h) for any stone. Compare with the motion equation v squared = 2 g h. Same answer, easier route.
Be careful with these

Energy is 'used up'. It is converted, not destroyed. A phone charger just moves energy around and wastes some as heat. Work is any effort. In physics, no motion along the force, no work. Power equals energy. A weak motor can lift a heavy load over a long time; a strong one does it faster. Same energy, different power.
Bhakra and your electricity unit

Hydroelectric dams are conservation of energy in action: water stored high (PE) falls through turbines (KE) and spins generators. The Bhakra Dam on the Sutlej, completed in the early 1960s, is among India's tallest gravity dams, and Jawaharlal Nehru called such dams the 'temples of modern India'. Every Indian household bill is in kWh, the same 3.6 million joules in the example above. When you use a 1000 W heater for an hour, you pay for exactly one unit.
Key takeaways

Work W = F d cos(theta), measured in joules. KE = (1/2) m v squared; PE = m g h. Total energy is conserved; friction turns it to heat. Power = work / time, in watts. 1 kWh = 3.6 million J. Think about it 1. Why does doubling a car's speed quadruple its braking distance? 2. A roller coaster's second hill is never taller than the first. Why?
Momentum and Collisions
Why crumple zones save lives

A truck is harder to stop than a bicycle at the same speed. A bullet is hard to stop even though it is tiny. Both facts are captured by one idea: momentum . Momentum explains collisions, rocket flight, airbags and why a cricketer pulls their hands back when catching a fast ball. It is also one of nature's strictest conserved quantities.
Momentum: mass in motion

Momentum p = m v Momentum is a vector with units kg m/s. A 1000 kg car at 20 m/s has p = 20,000 kg m/s. A 0.01 kg bullet at 400 m/s has only 4 kg m/s, but it can be stopped by a thin wall because the stopping time is tiny and the force is concentrated. Newton actually wrote his second law as: force = rate of change of momentum.
Impulse: a push over a time

Impulse F x t = change in momentum To change momentum you need force acting for some time. The same change can come from a big force for a short time or a small force for a long time. Catching a fast ball, you move your hands back, lengthening the time. The force drops and your palms are spared. Airbags and crumple zones do the same: they stretch the stopping time so the force on you is smaller.
Conservation of momentum

If no outside force acts on a system, its total momentum stays the same. In a collision, whatever momentum one body loses, the other gains. This follows from Newton's third law: during a collision the two forces are equal and opposite for the same time, so the momentum changes are equal and opposite. A rocket works this way too. Gas goes backwards with momentum; the rocket gains equal momentum forwards. No air needed.
Elastic and inelastic collisions

Momentum is conserved in every collision (without outside forces). Kinetic energy is not. Elastic: kinetic energy is also conserved. Billiard balls and gas molecules are close to this. Inelastic: some KE becomes heat, sound and deformation. Most real collisions. Perfectly inelastic: the bodies stick together, losing the most KE.
Two cars lock together

A 1000 kg car at 20 m/s hits an identical car at rest and they stick together (see diagram). Momentum before: 1000 x 20 = 20,000. After: 2000 x v. So v = 10 m/s . Kinetic energy before: (1/2) x 1000 x 400 = 200,000 J. After: (1/2) x 2000 x 100 = 100,000 J. Half the energy has gone into crumpling metal and heat. Momentum was conserved; energy was not.
The cricket bat

A 0.16 kg ball arrives at 40 m/s and is hit straight back at 40 m/s. Change in momentum = 0.16 x (40 + 40) = 12.8 kg m/s. If the ball touches the bat for 4 ms (0.004 s), the average force is 12.8 / 0.004 = 3200 N , about the weight of a 330 kg object. Such a short contact time is why the bat feels a sharp sting.
Frequent errors

'Momentum and kinetic energy are the same thing.' Momentum is mv and has direction; KE is (1/2)mv squared and does not. 'In a crash the bigger vehicle feels the bigger force.' The forces are equal. The lighter vehicle just gets the larger change in velocity. 'Energy is conserved in all collisions.' Total energy is, but mechanical energy usually is not.
Rockets and the cricket field

Every ISRO launch relies on conservation of momentum: the exhaust of the PSLV pushes it up. Staging, where empty stages drop away, lowers the mass so the same thrust gives a larger acceleration. On the cricket field, a fielder 'giving' with the ball is the impulse idea. Safety designers of Indian road vehicles use crumple zones and airbags built on the same physics, and India's crash-test programme, Bharat NCAP, began in 2023 to rate vehicles on such safety.
Key takeaways

Momentum p = mv is a vector, in kg m/s. Impulse (force x time) equals change in momentum. Total momentum is conserved when no outside force acts. Elastic collisions also keep kinetic energy; inelastic ones do not. Think about it 1. Why does a gun recoil backward when it fires a bullet? 2. Why is it better to land on sand than on concrete when you jump?
Rotation and Angular Momentum
Spinning things behave differently

A skater pulls her arms in and spins faster. A cat falls upside down and lands on its feet. A spinning top stands up when it should fall. A bicycle stays upright because its wheels spin. These all come from the physics of rotation. It mirrors the physics of straight-line motion, with new names: torque instead of force, moment of inertia instead of mass, angular momentum instead of momentum.
Describing rotation

We measure angles in radians : one full turn is 2 x pi (about 6.28) radians. Angular velocity (omega) is how many radians per second. A wheel making one turn per second has omega = 6.28 rad/s. A point at distance r from the axis moves with speed v = r x omega. So the rim of a wheel moves faster than a point near the hub, though both turn together.
Torque: the twist of a force

Torque torque = force x perpendicular distance from the axis You open a door by pushing far from the hinges, not near them. Same force, longer lever arm, more torque. A long spanner loosens a tight nut for the same reason. Archimedes is said to have boasted that with a long enough lever he could move the Earth. Torque is the principle behind it.
Moment of inertia: rotation's 'mass'

Mass resists a change in straight-line motion. Moment of inertia (I) resists a change in spin. It depends on how the mass is spread: mass far from the axis counts much more. Rotational second law torque = I x angular acceleration For a point mass, I = m r squared. A solid disc spins up more easily than a ring of the same mass, because the ring has all its mass at the edge.
Angular momentum and its conservation

Angular momentum L = I x omega If no outside torque acts, L stays constant. A skater spinning with arms out has a large I. Pulling arms in cuts I, so omega must rise to keep L the same. This is why a collapsing star spins faster as it shrinks, producing the rapidly spinning neutron stars we call pulsars.
Rolling and the kinetic energy of spin

A rolling wheel has two energies: motion of its centre, (1/2) m v squared, and spin, (1/2) I omega squared. On a slope, a solid ball beats a hollow ring in a race, because less of its energy goes into spin. This also explains why a gyroscope or spinning top resists tilting: its angular momentum wants to stay pointing the same way. Gyroscopes guide aircraft and ships.
The spinning skater

A skater spins at 2 rad/s with I = 4 kg m squared. She pulls her arms in so I = 1 kg m squared. Conservation: I1 x omega1 = I2 x omega2, so 4 x 2 = 1 x omega2, giving omega2 = 8 rad/s , four times faster. Her rotational energy goes from (1/2) x 4 x 4 = 8 J to (1/2) x 1 x 64 = 32 J. The extra energy comes from her muscles pulling her arms inwards.
Common errors

'Torque is just force.' No. It also depends on where you push. A force through the axis gives no torque at all. 'Bigger mass always means bigger I.' I depends on the spread of mass, not only its amount. 'Angular momentum is lost when the skater speeds up.' It stays the same; the spin rate and I trade off.
The potter's wheel and the satellite

India's traditional potter's wheel, the chaak of the kumhar, is a heavy flywheel. Its large moment of inertia stores spin, so it keeps turning smoothly between pushes of the potter's stick. Satellites, including Indian ones, often steer using spinning wheels inside them. Speeding up or slowing a wheel makes the satellite turn the other way, by conservation of angular momentum, with no fuel used.
Key takeaways

Torque = force x lever arm; it makes things rotate. Moment of inertia I depends on how mass is spread out from the axis. Angular momentum L = I omega is conserved without outside torque. Pulling mass inward speeds up rotation. Think about it 1. Why is a door handle placed far from the hinge? 2. Why does a cat twist its body and extend or retract its legs while falling?
Gravitation and Orbits
The force that holds the cosmos together

The same pull that drops an apple keeps the Moon circling Earth, Earth circling the Sun, and the Sun circling the Milky Way. Newton's great leap, around 1687, was to see that these are one thing. This idea gave humanity its first law that worked equally on Earth and in the sky, and today it guides every satellite and space probe.
Newton's law of gravitation

Universal gravitation F = G m1 m2 / r squared Every mass pulls every other mass. The pull grows with the masses and falls with the square of the distance. Double the distance and the force drops to one-quarter. G is a tiny constant, 6.67 x 10 to the power -11 in SI units. Henry Cavendish first measured it in 1798 with a delicate torsion balance. Gravity between everyday objects is too weak to notice; it only shows up when one body is as big as a planet.
Why g = 9.8 m/s squared

At the surface, a mass m feels F = G M m / R squared. Dividing by m gives the acceleration: Surface gravity g = G M / R squared For Earth, M is about 6 x 10 to the power 24 kg and R about 6.4 x 10 to the power 6 m, giving g near 9.8. Move higher and g shrinks with distance squared: at a height equal to Earth's radius (r = 2R), g is one-quarter. The Moon, with less mass and smaller size, has g of about 1.6, roughly one-sixth of Earth's.
Kepler's three laws

Johannes Kepler, studying Tycho Brahe's data, found three rules for planets: 1609: orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus. 1609: a line from Sun to planet sweeps equal areas in equal times, so planets move faster when closer. 1619: the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the average distance. Newton showed all three follow from his inverse-square law. That was a stunning proof.
Orbits: falling and missing

Imagine firing a cannonball sideways from a mountain. It curves down and lands. Fire it faster and it lands farther. Fire it fast enough, about 7.9 km/s near Earth's surface, and the ground curves away as fast as the ball falls. It never lands. That is an orbit. Orbital speed at distance r is v = square root of (G M / r). Farther orbits are slower. The International Space Station, about 400 km up, circles Earth in about 92 minutes, and its astronauts feel weightless because they are in continuous free fall.
Escape velocity and special orbits

To leave Earth for good, a rocket needs the escape velocity : v = square root of (2 G M / R), about 11.2 km/s. It does not depend on the rocket's mass. A satellite at about 35,786 km above the equator takes exactly one day to go round, matching Earth's spin. Seen from the ground it hovers in place. This is a geostationary orbit , used for communications and weather.
Gravity at 2 Earth radii

At the surface g = 9.8. If you are at distance r = 2R from Earth's centre (that is, one radius above the surface), g falls by 2 squared = 4. g = 9.8 / 4 = 2.45 m/s squared . A 60 kg person would weigh 60 x 9.8 = 588 N on the surface and 147 N at that height. Their mass stays 60 kg.
Space is not magic

'Astronauts float because there is no gravity.' At the ISS gravity is still about 90 percent of the surface value. They float because they are falling freely along with the station. 'Heavier planets must have bigger g.' g depends on M and R squared. A big, light planet can have weak surface gravity. 'The Sun's pull is only felt up close.' Gravity has infinite range; it just weakens.
Aryabhata, from astronomer to satellite

The astronomer Aryabhata (born 476 CE) wrote in the Aryabhatiya that the Earth rotates on its axis, explaining the apparent motion of stars. India's first satellite, launched by the Soviet Union on 19 April 1975, was named Aryabhata in his honour. Today India's INSAT and GSAT satellites sit in geostationary orbit at about 36,000 km, and Mangalyaan reached Mars orbit on 24 September 2014 on India's first try, using a gravity-assisted path planned with exactly these laws.
Key takeaways

F = G m1 m2 / r squared: weaker with the square of distance. Surface gravity g = G M / R squared. Kepler's laws describe planetary orbits; Newton explained them. Orbiting means falling around the planet; escape speed from Earth is 11.2 km/s. Think about it 1. If Earth's mass were doubled but its radius kept, what would happen to your weight? 2. Why must a geostationary satellite be at one particular height?
Fluids: Pressure, Buoyancy and Flow
Why does a ship float and a dam get thicker?

A steel ship weighs thousands of tonnes yet floats. A dam is far thicker at the bottom than the top. A small push on a car jack lifts a whole car. Aeroplanes stay up on air that you cannot see. All of these are the physics of fluids : liquids and gases, things that flow. Their key ideas are pressure, buoyancy and flow speed.
Pressure: force spread over area

Pressure P = F / A The unit is the pascal (Pa): one newton per square metre. A sharp knife cuts because a modest force is squeezed onto a tiny area. A camel's wide feet stop it sinking in sand for the opposite reason. Air presses on us too. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 101,000 Pa, called one atmosphere. We do not feel it because the fluids inside us push outward equally.
Pressure grows with depth

Pressure in a liquid P = (density) x g x h Deeper means more fluid above pressing down. For water, density is 1000 kg per cubic metre, so every 10 m of depth adds about one atmosphere. That is why divers feel pressure on their ears, and why dam walls are built thicker at the base. Notice that only depth matters, not the width of the container.
Pascal's law and the hydraulic lift

Blaise Pascal (1650s) found that pressure applied to a confined fluid is passed on equally in every direction. A small piston pushing on a small area creates a pressure; the same pressure on a big piston gives a big force. With areas 0.01 and 0.1 square metres, a 100 N push becomes 1000 N. This is how car jacks, garage lifts and the brakes of vehicles work. (You gain force, not energy: the small piston moves ten times farther.)
Buoyancy: Archimedes' principle

Archimedes of Syracuse (around 250 BCE) found that a body in a fluid feels an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid it pushes aside. Buoyant force F = (fluid density) x V x g If this force beats the body's weight, it floats. A steel ship floats because its hollow shape displaces a huge volume of water, so its average density is less than water's. The same steel as a solid block would sink.
Flow and Bernoulli's principle

For a steady flow of liquid in a pipe, what goes in must come out: A x v is constant. Narrow the pipe and the water speeds up, as when you put a thumb over a hose. Daniel Bernoulli (1738) showed that where a fluid moves faster, its pressure is lower: Bernoulli P + (1/2) density v squared + density g h = constant This helps explain lift on an aircraft wing, spray bottles and the way a curveball curves.
Pressure 10 m under water

P = density x g x h = 1000 x 9.8 x 10 = 98,000 Pa , about one atmosphere added by the water. Total pressure at 10 m = surface air pressure + this = 101,000 + 98,000, nearly 2 atmospheres . Buoyancy check: a 0.002 cubic metre (2 litre) bottle, fully under water, feels an upthrust of 1000 x 0.002 x 9.8 = 19.6 N, which is why it pops upward when you let go.
Fluid facts people get wrong

'Heavy things sink, light things float.' It is about density. A huge ship floats; a small steel pin sinks. 'Water pressure depends on how much water there is.' It depends on depth. A deep narrow tube and a wide lake of the same depth give the same pressure. 'Faster air pushes harder.' The reverse: faster fluid has lower pressure along a streamline.
Dams and aircraft carriers

The Bhakra Dam is thicker at its base since the water pressure there is much greater. India's hydropower and irrigation dams, from Hirakud to Sardar Sarovar, are designed with the P = density x g x h equation in mind. The Indian Navy's ships, including the aircraft carrier INS Vikrant (commissioned 2022), float by Archimedes' principle: the carrier displaces water equal to its own huge weight.
Key takeaways

Pressure P = F/A; in a liquid P = density x g x h. Pascal's law: pressure in a closed fluid spreads equally, giving hydraulic force multiplication. Buoyant force equals the weight of fluid displaced. Faster flow means lower pressure (Bernoulli). Think about it 1. Why does a hot-air balloon rise, in terms of buoyancy? 2. Why is it harder to open a door to a pressurised cabin than an ordinary door?
Oscillations and Simple Harmonic Motion
Everything that swings, hums or ticks

A child on a swing, a plucked guitar string, a clock pendulum, atoms in a crystal, a bridge in the wind. Countless systems wobble back and forth around a resting position. The simplest, and the most important, kind of wobble is simple harmonic motion (SHM). Once you understand it, you understand the heart of sound, light, radio, quantum physics and clocks.
The restoring force

SHM happens when a force pulls an object back toward the centre, and the pull grows in proportion to how far it has been pushed away. Hooke's law for a spring: Hooke's law F = - k x x is the displacement; k is the stiffness (N/m); the minus sign says the force opposes the displacement. Stretch right, it pulls left. Pass the centre, it pulls the other way. The result is endless oscillation.
Amplitude, period and frequency

Amplitude (A) is the largest distance from the centre. Period (T) is the time for one full cycle. Frequency (f) is cycles per second, in hertz (Hz). Link f = 1 / T If one swing takes 2 s, the frequency is 0.5 Hz. Plotted against time, the position makes a smooth wave called a sine curve.
Spring and pendulum formulas

Period formulas Mass on a spring: T = 2 pi x square root of (m / k) Simple pendulum: T = 2 pi x square root of (L / g) A heavier mass on a spring swings more slowly; a stiffer spring swings faster. For the pendulum, only the length and g matter. The mass of the bob does not enter, and (for small swings) neither does the amplitude. Galileo noticed this around 1583 watching a swinging lamp, and Huygens used it to build the first accurate pendulum clock in 1656.
Energy sloshes back and forth

At the ends of the swing the object stops for an instant: all its energy is potential (stored). At the centre it moves fastest: all energy is kinetic. In between the energy is shared. The total, (1/2) k A squared, stays constant if there is no friction. In real life, damping slowly drains the energy as heat, and oscillations die away unless you keep pushing, as a parent does to a swing.
Resonance: pushing at the right rhythm

Every oscillator has a natural frequency. If you drive it at that frequency, even gentle pushes add up and the amplitude grows enormously. This is resonance . It is how a child gets higher on a swing, how a radio tunes to a station, and how a singer can shatter a glass. It can also destroy: the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in the USA twisted apart in wind in 1940. Soldiers break step on bridges for the same reason.
A pendulum and a spring

Pendulum of length 1 m: T = 2 pi x square root of (1/9.8) = 6.28 x 0.32 = 2.0 s . A 'seconds pendulum' takes one second per swing, so its full period is 2 s, with length close to one metre. Spring with m = 0.5 kg and k = 200 N/m: T = 6.28 x square root of (0.5/200) = 6.28 x 0.05 = 0.31 s , so f is about 3.2 Hz. On the Moon (g about 1.6) the same pendulum would take 2 pi x square root of (1/1.6) = 4.9 s: slower.
Where people slip

'A heavier pendulum swings slower.' Not so; mass cancels out for a pendulum. 'Acceleration is zero at the ends.' It is largest at the ends, where the restoring force is biggest. It is zero at the centre. 'Bigger swing, longer period.' For small swings, the period does not depend on amplitude.
Raman and the tabla

C. V. Raman studied the vibrations of Indian drums and strings. In the 1920s he showed that the tabla and mridangam produce nearly harmonic overtones, because of the loaded circle of paste on the drum skin. That is why these instruments sound so tuneful, unlike most drums. The sitar, tanpura and veena also rely on string vibration and resonance of their hollow gourds. Raman received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930 for a different discovery, on light scattering.
Key takeaways

SHM arises when the restoring force is proportional to displacement: F = -kx. Period T = 2 pi x square root of (m/k) for a spring; T = 2 pi x square root of (L/g) for a pendulum. Frequency f = 1/T, measured in hertz. Energy swaps between kinetic and potential; resonance builds large oscillations. Think about it 1. Why would a grandfather clock run slow at the top of a high mountain? 2. Why do marching soldiers break step crossing a bridge?
Waves and Sound
How a voice crosses a room

When you speak, nothing travels from your mouth to a friend's ear except a disturbance. The air itself only jiggles in place. The pattern of the jiggle moves on, passing the message from molecule to molecule. That is a wave : energy travelling without matter travelling. Sound, ripples, earthquakes, radio, light and even the waves of quantum physics all share this behaviour.
Two kinds of waves

Transverse waves shake the medium at right angles to the wave's direction. A rope flicked up and down, or water ripples. Light is also transverse. Longitudinal waves push and pull along the direction of travel, creating squeezed regions (compressions) and stretched regions (rarefactions). Sound in air is longitudinal. Sound needs a medium (air, water, steel). It cannot cross empty space, which is why space is silent.
The wave equation

Wave speed v = f x wavelength Frequency f (waves per second) times wavelength (length of one wave) gives the speed. The speed is set by the medium; the source sets the frequency. So higher frequency means shorter wavelength, at the same speed.
Sound: pitch, loudness and speed

Pitch is frequency: a high note has high f. Humans hear roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Loudness depends on amplitude and is measured in decibels (dB): ordinary talk is about 60 dB, and sound above about 85 dB over long periods can harm hearing. In air at 20 degrees C sound travels at about 343 m/s . It is faster in water (about 1500 m/s) and faster still in steel (over 5000 m/s).
Superposition, interference and beats

When waves meet, they simply add. Two crests make a bigger crest (constructive); a crest meeting a trough cancels (destructive). Two notes of slightly different frequencies, such as 440 and 444 Hz, make a throbbing sound at 4 beats per second. Musicians use this to tune instruments: when the beats vanish, the notes match. Noise-cancelling headphones use destructive interference on purpose.
The Doppler effect and standing waves

When a source moves toward you, waves bunch up and the pitch rises; when it moves away, the pitch drops. Think of an ambulance siren passing. Christian Doppler predicted this in 1842. A string fixed at both ends supports standing waves at special frequencies: the fundamental and its multiples (harmonics). Guitars, flutes and organ pipes make music from these. Radar guns and weather radar use the Doppler shift too.
Tuning note and thunder

Concert A is 440 Hz. In air at 343 m/s, wavelength = 343 / 440 = 0.78 m . Thunder: light reaches you almost instantly, sound takes time. If you hear thunder 3 s after the flash, the lightning is about 343 x 3 = 1030 m, roughly 1 km away. Each 3 seconds of delay is about one kilometre. An echo returning from a wall after 0.2 s means the wall is 343 x 0.2 / 2 = 34 m away (half, since the sound goes there and back).
Sound and wave mix-ups

'Sound travels faster when louder.' Speed depends on the medium, not loudness or pitch. 'Sound is fastest in air because air is light.' It is faster in denser, stiffer media like steel. 'The wave carries the water or air along.' The particles only oscillate; the energy moves on.
Doppler radar and the Indian ear

The India Meteorological Department uses Doppler weather radars to track the winds inside cyclones by the shift in frequency of reflected waves. This gives hours of warning before landfall. Indian classical music builds on exact frequency ratios and resonance. C. V. Raman's work on the harmonics of the tabla and mridangam showed why their sound is so musical. The Indian Navy and fishermen also use sonar, sound pulses and echoes, to find objects under water.
Key takeaways

Waves carry energy, not matter. They are transverse or longitudinal. v = f x wavelength. Sound in air travels at about 343 m/s; it needs a medium. Waves interfere; the Doppler effect shifts frequency for moving sources. Think about it 1. Why does your voice sound deeper to you when you speak than on a recording? 2. If you shout in a canyon and hear the echo after 4 s, how wide is the canyon?
Temperature, Heat and Kinetic Theory
Hot and cold, explained by motion

Touch a cup of tea and it feels hot; hold an ice cube and it feels cold. For centuries people thought heat was a fluid called 'caloric'. Today we know something stranger and simpler: heat is the jiggling of atoms. This lesson connects the everyday words (temperature, heat, boiling, melting) to the unseen dance of molecules. It also explains why the monsoon blows and why a clay pot keeps water cool.
Temperature measures average jiggle

Temperature tells how energetic the random motion of molecules is, on average. Hotter means faster jiggling. We use three scales. Celsius sets water's freezing at 0 and boiling at 100. Fahrenheit (used in the US) has them at 32 and 212. Scientists use kelvin : K = C + 273.15. Zero kelvin, or -273.15 C, is absolute zero , where molecular motion is at its minimum. Nothing can be colder.
Heat is energy on the move

Temperature is not heat. Heat is the energy that flows from a hot body to a cold one because of a temperature difference. It is measured in joules. A bathtub of warm water has a lower temperature than a boiling spoonful, yet holds far more heat. James Joule showed in the 1840s that work and heat are interchangeable: stirring water with paddles warms it. Heat is just one form of energy.
Specific heat and latent heat

Heating a substance Q = m x c x (change in temperature) c is the specific heat. For water, c = 4186 J per kg per degree, unusually high. Water takes a lot of heat to warm up and releases a lot as it cools. While ice melts or water boils, the temperature stays flat: the heat goes into breaking bonds, not speeding molecules. This is latent heat . Melting ice needs about 334,000 J/kg; boiling water needs about 2,260,000 J/kg.
Kinetic theory of gases

A gas is a swarm of tiny particles flying about and bouncing off walls. Their bouncing is pressure. Their average kinetic energy is proportional to temperature: roughly (3/2) k T per molecule, where k is Boltzmann's constant. This gives the ideal gas law: Ideal gas law P V = n R T Heat a gas in a closed container and the pressure rises. Squeeze it and the pressure rises. This links the big picture (P, V, T) to the atomic one.
Three ways heat moves

Conduction: energy passes through touching atoms. A metal spoon in hot tea warms up. Metals conduct well; wood, air and wool poorly. Convection: a fluid carries heat as it moves. Warm air rises; cooler air sinks. This forms sea breezes and drives weather. Radiation: electromagnetic waves carry heat, even across empty space. That is how the Sun warms us.
Heating and boiling a kilogram of water

Warm 1 kg of water from 20 C to 100 C: Q = 1 x 4186 x 80 = 335,000 J . Now boil it all away: Q = 1 x 2,260,000 = 2,260,000 J . Boiling needs nearly seven times more energy than heating to the boiling point. This is why steam burns are worse than boiling-water burns, since condensing steam dumps this huge latent heat on your skin.
Hot and cold confusions

'Cold flows into things.' There is only heat flow, from hot to cold. A cold drink gains heat. 'Temperature and heat are the same.' Temperature is a level; heat is energy transferred. 'Boiling water keeps getting hotter if you turn the flame up.' At normal pressure it stays at 100 C; extra heat just boils it faster.
The monsoon and the matka

Water's high specific heat means the sea warms slowly, while land warms fast in the Indian summer. Hot land air rises and cooler, moist air from the Indian Ocean rushes in: the southwest monsoon that brings India most of its rain. A clay matka stays cool because water seeps through and evaporates from the surface. Evaporation needs latent heat, taken from the water inside. S. N. Bose later developed, in 1924, the statistics used to describe quantum gases, extending the kinetic picture into the quantum world.
Key takeaways

Temperature is average molecular motion; K = C + 273.15. Heat is energy transferred by temperature difference. Q = m c change in T; latent heat powers melting and boiling. Gases obey PV = nRT, explained by kinetic theory. Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation. Think about it 1. Why does a metal chair feel colder than a wooden one at the same temperature? 2. Why does a wet cloth around a bottle cool it?
The Laws of Thermodynamics
Why you can't build a perpetual-motion machine

Inventors have long dreamed of a machine that runs forever, or that turns heat from the sea into free power for ships. Nature says no, and the laws that say it are among the most reliable in all of science. Einstein once said thermodynamics is the one theory he was sure would never be overthrown, within its domain. The laws are short, but they limit every engine, fridge and power station on Earth.
The zeroth law: temperature makes sense

If body A is in thermal equilibrium with C, and B is in equilibrium with C, then A and B are in equilibrium with each other. It sounds obvious, but it is what makes a thermometer meaningful: two things at the same reading will not exchange heat. It was named 'zeroth' later, since it was seen as more basic than the first law, which was already numbered.
First law: energy is conserved

First law change in internal energy = Q - W Heat Q added to a system either raises its internal energy or is turned into work W done by the system. Energy is never created or destroyed. Compress a bicycle pump quickly and the air gets hot: work done on the gas raises its energy. Julius Mayer and James Joule established this idea in the 1840s, showing heat and work are the same kind of thing.
Second law: heat flows downhill

Heat flows by itself from hot to cold, never the reverse. A cup of tea cools; it never spontaneously heats up by draining warmth from the room. Two classic statements: Clausius (1850): no process can have the sole result of moving heat from cold to hot. Kelvin-Planck: no engine can turn heat entirely into work with nothing wasted. Some heat must always be rejected to a cold reservoir.
Heat engines and Carnot's limit

A heat engine takes heat Qh from a hot source, does work W, and throws out heat Qc to a cold sink. Efficiency = W / Qh. Sadi Carnot (1824) showed that the best possible engine between temperatures Th and Tc (in kelvin) has: Carnot efficiency efficiency = 1 - Tc / Th The hotter the source and the colder the sink, the better. No real engine can beat this.
Refrigerators and the third law

A fridge is an engine running backwards: it uses work to pump heat from cold inside to warm outside. The back of your fridge is warm for this reason. An air-conditioner does the same. The third law says you can never reach absolute zero, 0 K, in a finite number of steps. Scientists have reached billionths of a kelvin above it, but never zero itself.
Best possible engine

An engine runs between 500 K and 300 K. Maximum efficiency = 1 - 300/500 = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4, or 40 percent . If it takes in Qh = 1000 J, the most work it can give is W = 400 J, and it must reject Qc = 600 J (see the diagram). A real engine does worse, perhaps 25 to 30 percent, because of friction and heat leaks. Check with the first law: Qh = W + Qc, so 1000 = 400 + 600.
Where thinking goes wrong

'A fridge with the door open cools the room.' It heats it. The fridge pumps heat out of the box but also adds its motor's energy, so the room warms. '100 percent efficient engines just need better design.' The second law forbids it, even in theory. 'The first law means I cannot run out of useful energy.' Total energy is conserved, but useful energy is not: it degrades into spread-out heat.
India's power plants and cooling

Most of India's electricity still comes from coal-fired thermal plants, which are heat engines: coal heats steam, steam spins a turbine. Their efficiency is typically around one-third to 40 percent, close to what Carnot's law allows for their temperatures. The rest leaves as heat in cooling towers and chimneys. India's rapid growth in air-conditioning, which moves heat out of homes, is a major source of rising power demand. Efficient (higher star-rated) units do the same cooling with less work.
Key takeaways

Zeroth: equal temperature means thermal equilibrium; this defines thermometers. First: energy is conserved, change in U = Q - W. Second: heat flows hot to cold; no engine is 100 percent efficient. Carnot efficiency = 1 - Tc/Th (in kelvin). Third: absolute zero cannot be reached. Think about it 1. Why does raising the steam temperature in a power plant improve efficiency? 2. Why can't you cool your kitchen by leaving the fridge door open?
Entropy and the Arrow of Time
Why a film run backwards looks wrong

Watch a film of an egg falling and splattering, then run it backwards: you laugh, because it cannot happen. Yet Newton's laws work equally well in both directions. A ball bouncing backwards in time obeys the same laws. So what makes the past different from the future? The answer is entropy , and it is one of the deepest ideas in physics: the arrow of time comes from the way things spread out.
Entropy as spread-out-ness

The word entropy was coined by Rudolf Clausius in 1865. Loosely, entropy measures how spread out energy is, or how many ways the parts of a system can be arranged without changing how it looks overall. A tidy deck of cards has few arrangements. A shuffled deck has an astronomical number. Shuffling raises entropy. Hot coffee cooling into a room spreads its energy over many more molecules: entropy rises.
Boltzmann's counting

Ludwig Boltzmann (1870s) gave the precise meaning: Boltzmann's entropy S = k x ln(W) W is the number of microscopic arrangements (microstates) that give the same large-scale look; k is Boltzmann's constant, 1.38 x 10 to the power -23 J/K; ln is the natural logarithm. This formula is engraved on his tombstone in Vienna. More ways means higher entropy. Nature is not driven to disorder by a force; disorder simply has overwhelmingly more ways to happen.
The second law, restated

The entropy of an isolated system never decreases. It rises in all real processes, and stays the same only in ideal, perfectly reversible ones. For heat Q flowing at temperature T, the entropy change is Q / T. Heat leaving a hot body lowers its entropy a little; heat entering a cold body raises it more. The net is a gain, so heat flowing hot to cold is allowed and the reverse is not.
Why the arrow of time exists

Imagine 100 gas molecules in a box, all in the left half. Opening a partition, they spread out. The chance that they all return to the left by themselves is (1/2) to the power 100, about 8 x 10 to the power -31. For a real gas, with 10 to the power 23 molecules, the odds are beyond zero for any practical purpose. So the past is the direction in which entropy was lower. The question of why the early universe had such low entropy remains an open problem.
Life, order and the cosmos

Living things are highly ordered, so do they break the law? No. A plant takes in low-entropy sunlight and gives off high-entropy heat. Earth's local order is paid for by a larger entropy increase elsewhere, mostly in the Sun's spreading light. Looking far ahead, the universe may drift toward a state of maximum entropy, with all energy evenly spread, the so-called heat death . Physicists also link entropy to information: Claude Shannon's 1948 information theory uses a very similar formula.
Heat flowing between bodies

1000 J of heat flows from a body at 400 K to one at 300 K. Hot body loses entropy: -1000/400 = -2.5 J/K. Cold body gains entropy: +1000/300 = +3.33 J/K. Net change = +0.83 J/K , positive, so the process is allowed. Try the reverse (cold to hot): the net would be -0.83 J/K, negative, so it never happens on its own.
Entropy myths

'Entropy just means messiness.' Useful as a picture, but the precise idea is counting microstates and the spread of energy. 'Life violates the second law.' Only isolated systems must not lose entropy; living things are open systems. 'Entropy can never decrease anywhere.' It can decrease locally (a freezer making ice) if more entropy is created elsewhere.
Bose, Saha and counting states

Satyendra Nath Bose's 1924 paper from Dhaka showed how to count the microstates of light particles correctly; Einstein translated and promoted it. The result, Bose-Einstein statistics , led to the idea of the boson, named after him, and to the Bose-Einstein condensate, first made in a lab in 1995. Meghnad Saha used thermodynamics and statistics in 1920 to explain how atoms ionise in hot stars. The Saha equation lets us read the temperature of distant stars from their light.
Key takeaways

Entropy counts the ways a system can be arranged: S = k ln W. The entropy of an isolated system never decreases. This gives time its direction; it is statistics, not a force. Local order, like life, is paid for by entropy increases elsewhere. Think about it 1. Why does a stirred cup of milk and tea never un-mix? 2. A freezer lowers the entropy of water turning to ice. Where does the extra entropy go?
Electric Charge and Fields
The force behind almost everything you touch

Static cling, a spark from a doorknob, lightning, a phone screen, even why you do not fall through the floor: all are electric forces. Gravity holds planets together, but between atoms and molecules, electric force rules, and it is vastly stronger. Understanding charge and its field is the first step to all of electronics, chemistry and biology.
Electric charge

Matter carries a property called charge , of two kinds, named positive and negative by Benjamin Franklin. Like charges repel; unlike charges attract. Charge comes in tiny lumps: the electron carries -1.6 x 10 to the power -19 coulomb, the proton +1.6 x 10 to the power -19. This is quantisation . Charge is also conserved : it can move around but the total never changes. Rub a plastic comb on hair: electrons move from hair to comb, so neither gains charge from nothing.
Conductors and insulators

In a conductor such as copper, some electrons are free to roam, so charge moves easily. In an insulator such as rubber, glass or dry air, electrons stay put. That is why wires are copper wrapped in plastic. Charge on a conductor sits on its outer surface, and inside a hollow metal shell the field is zero. This is why you are safe in a car during a thunderstorm: the metal body acts as a shield.
Coulomb's law

Charles-Augustin de Coulomb measured in 1785 how charges push and pull: Coulomb's law F = k x q1 x q2 / r squared k = 9 x 10 to the power 9 (in SI units) It is an inverse-square law, just like gravity: double the distance and the force falls to one-quarter. But electric force is hugely stronger. Between a proton and an electron it beats gravity by about 10 to the power 39.
The electric field

Instead of thinking of charges acting at a distance, physicists picture each charge filling space with a field . The field E at a point is the force a small test charge would feel, per unit charge: Electric field E = F / q Units: newtons per coulomb. Field lines show direction: they start on positive charge and end on negative. Where lines crowd together, the field is strong.
Gauss's law and point charges

Carl Friedrich Gauss showed that the total field passing out through any closed surface depends only on the charge inside. It is a powerful shortcut. For a single point charge Q the field at distance r is E = k Q / r squared. Outside a charged sphere the field looks exactly as if all the charge sat at the centre. Between two oppositely charged parallel plates, the field is uniform: the same size and direction everywhere in between.
Two microcoulomb charges

Two charges of 1 microcoulomb (10 to the power -6 C) are 0.1 m apart. F = 9 x 10 to the power 9 x (10 to the power -6) x (10 to the power -6) / (0.1) squared = 9 x 10 to the power -3 / 0.01 = 0.9 N . Move them to 0.2 m apart and the force drops to 0.225 N, one-quarter. The field of the first charge at 0.1 m is E = 9 x 10 to the power 9 x 10 to the power -6 / 0.01 = 900,000 N/C.
Charge confusions

'Rubbing creates charge.' It only moves existing charge from one body to the other. 'Field lines are real threads.' They are a drawing aid for the direction and strength of the field. 'Neutral objects feel no force.' A charged comb attracts neutral paper bits by shifting their charge slightly (polarisation).
Lightning in India

India sees thousands of lightning strikes every year, and lightning kills many people, especially farmers in open fields in states such as Bihar, Odisha and Uttar Pradesh. The India Meteorological Department now issues lightning warnings. A lightning rod (conductor) on a building, invented by Franklin, gives the charge an easy path to the ground. In the open, crouch low and avoid trees; inside a car or a pucca building you are far safer. A thundercloud builds up enormous charge differences, often hundreds of millions of volts.
Key takeaways

Charge is of two kinds, quantised and conserved. Coulomb's law: F = k q1 q2 / r squared. Electric field E = F/q; lines go from + to -. Conductors let charge move; insulators do not. Think about it 1. Why does a balloon rubbed on hair stick to a wall? 2. Why do fuel tankers trail a metal chain on the ground?
Electric Potential and Capacitors
Storing electricity in a sandwich

The flash of a camera delivers a burst of light far brighter than a small battery could give instantly. A doctor's defibrillator shocks a stopped heart. Both use a device that stores charge slowly and releases it fast: the capacitor . To understand it we first need electric potential , the 'height' of the electric landscape that makes charge move.
Electric potential energy

Pushing a positive charge toward another positive charge is like pushing a ball uphill: you do work, and the charge stores potential energy . Let go and it flies away, converting that energy to motion. This is exactly like gravity, with charge taking the role of mass. The electric force is conservative, so we can assign a potential energy to every position.
Potential and voltage

Potential V = U / q Electric potential is energy per unit charge. Its unit is the volt (V): one joule per coulomb, named for Alessandro Volta. A 1.5 V cell gives each coulomb of charge 1.5 J. What matters in practice is the potential difference between two points, the voltage. Charge flows from high to low potential, like water flowing downhill. A bird on a bare power line is safe: no voltage difference across its feet.
Field and potential are linked

In a uniform field, potential changes steadily with distance: Uniform field E = V / d So the unit of field can also be volts per metre. Where the potential changes quickly with distance, the field is strong. A voltage of 12 V across 1 cm gives a field of 1200 V/m. Surfaces of equal potential are equipotentials . Field lines always cross them at right angles, and no work is done moving a charge along one.
The capacitor

A capacitor is two conductors separated by a gap (often an insulator). Connect it to a battery: charge +Q builds on one plate and -Q on the other. Capacitance C = Q / V C = (e0 x A) / d for parallel plates The unit of C is the farad (F), named for Michael Faraday; real capacitors are microfarads. Bigger plates and a smaller gap store more. A material (dielectric) between the plates raises C further.
Energy stored and series or parallel

A charged capacitor stores energy: U = (1/2) C V squared. The energy sits in the electric field between the plates. Capacitors in parallel add up: C = C1 + C2 (bigger plate area). In series , 1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2 (effectively a larger gap). They block steady current but pass changing signals, which is why they appear in filters, tuners and power supplies.
A 10 microfarad capacitor on 12 V

Charge: Q = C V = 10 x 10 to the power -6 x 12 = 1.2 x 10 to the power -4 C (120 microcoulombs). Energy: U = (1/2) x 10 x 10 to the power -6 x 144 = 7.2 x 10 to the power -4 J (0.72 millijoule). Joined with a 10 microfarad one in parallel, total C = 20 microfarads; in series, 5 microfarads.
Capacitor and voltage errors

'Voltage is a thing that flows.' Voltage is a difference in potential, like a height difference; charge flows because of it. 'A capacitor is a battery.' A battery makes charge flow through chemistry for hours. A capacitor stores a small amount and releases it quickly. 'High voltage always means danger.' Static shock can be thousands of volts but carries tiny charge; current and energy decide the harm.
The ceiling fan and the touchscreen

Almost every Indian ceiling fan has a small capacitor in its housing. It shifts the phase of the current in one winding so that the single-phase motor starts turning. When the fan slows or hums, a failing capacitor is the first suspect. Your smartphone's touchscreen is a grid of tiny capacitors; a finger changes the capacitance at one point, and the phone finds where you touched. India is one of the world's largest smartphone markets.
Key takeaways

Potential is energy per unit charge; voltage is a potential difference. 1 V = 1 J/C. In a uniform field, E = V/d. Capacitance C = Q/V; stored energy = (1/2) C V squared. Parallel capacitors add; series ones combine like resistors in parallel. Think about it 1. Why can a bird sit safely on a high-voltage wire? 2. How would you raise a capacitor's capacitance without changing its size?
Current, Resistance and Circuits
From a battery to the whole grid

Every phone, light bulb, fan and train runs on electric current moving through circuits. The rules of circuits are simple enough that you can learn them in an hour, yet they power the digital world. The central idea: voltage pushes, resistance resists, current is the result.
Current: charge in motion

Current I = Q / t Current is the amount of charge passing a point per second. The unit is the ampere (A): one coulomb per second. A phone charger may give 2 A; a household bulb draws a fraction of an amp. By convention current is drawn flowing from positive to negative, though in wires it is actually electrons drifting the other way, slowly, at about a millimetre per second. The signal moves fast because the whole 'sea' of electrons shifts together.
Ohm's law and resistance

Ohm's law V = I x R Georg Ohm found in 1827 that, for many conductors, current is proportional to voltage. The constant is resistance R, in ohms. A larger voltage drives more current; a larger resistance allows less. Resistance of a wire: R = (resistivity) x length / area. Long, thin wires resist more; thick, short ones less. Copper has very low resistivity, so it is used for wiring.
Series circuits

In a series circuit, components are in a single chain. The same current passes through each, and resistances add: R = R1 + R2. The battery voltage divides among them in proportion to their resistance. If one bulb in a cheap string of series lights burns out, the whole chain goes dark, because the loop is broken. That is the key weakness of series wiring.
Parallel circuits

In a parallel circuit, each component has its own branch across the same voltage. Currents add; resistances combine as 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2. Adding branches lowers the total resistance. Homes are wired in parallel, so each appliance gets the full mains voltage and works independently. Switch one off and the others keep running. Gustav Kirchhoff's rules (1845) make all this precise: current in equals current out at a junction; voltages around a loop sum to zero.
Power and heating

Electric power P = V x I = I squared x R = V squared / R The watt again: joules per second. Current through resistance makes heat (Joule heating): useful in a geyser or iron, a waste in power lines. A fuse is a thin wire that melts if too much current flows, protecting the circuit. A modern MCB switch does the same job.
A 12 V battery with 4 and 2 ohm resistors

Series: R = 4 + 2 = 6 ohms. Current I = 12 / 6 = 2 A (see the diagram). Voltage across the 4 ohm: 2 x 4 = 8 V; across the 2 ohm: 2 x 2 = 4 V. They add to 12 V. Power: 12 x 2 = 24 W . Now put them in parallel: 1/R = 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4, so R = 1.33 ohms and total current = 12 / 1.33 = 9 A. Far more current.
Circuit confusions

'Current is used up by a bulb.' The same current leaves as enters; it is energy that is converted to light and heat. 'Batteries supply a fixed current.' A battery gives roughly a fixed voltage; the current depends on the circuit. 'More resistors always mean more resistance.' In parallel they lower the total.
230 volts, 50 hertz

Indian homes receive alternating current at 230 V and 50 Hz. A typical 1500 W electric kettle draws about 6.5 A (1500 / 230), so it needs a heavier plug and wire than a small bulb. The earth pin and MCB in your home protect against shocks and overloads. India's solar push turns sunlight into DC electricity in panels, and the country's installed solar capacity has grown rapidly through the 2020s. Solar plants such as Bhadla in Rajasthan are among the world's largest.
Key takeaways

Current I = Q/t, measured in amperes. Ohm's law: V = IR. Series: same current, R adds. Parallel: same voltage, 1/R adds. Power P = VI = I squared R; fuses protect against overload. Think about it 1. Why do power lines carry high voltage rather than high current? 2. Why are household appliances wired in parallel?
Magnetism and Electromagnetic Induction
Electricity and magnetism are one thing

For centuries, electricity (amber and sparks) and magnetism (lodestones and compasses) looked like different subjects. Then, in the 1800s, experiments showed each makes the other. That discovery gave us electric motors, generators, transformers and eventually radio. Almost all the electricity you use is produced by moving a magnet near a coil of wire.
Magnets and magnetic fields

Every magnet has a north and south pole. Like poles repel; unlike attract. Cut a magnet in half and you get two smaller magnets, never a single pole: no magnetic monopole has ever been found. A magnet fills space with a magnetic field (B, measured in tesla), with lines running from north to south outside the magnet. A compass needle lines up with Earth's field because Earth itself acts like a giant magnet.
Oersted: currents make magnetic fields

In 1820, Hans Christian Oersted noticed a compass needle swing when a wire nearby carried current. Moving charge creates a magnetic field. A straight wire makes circular field lines around it. Wind the wire into a coil (a solenoid ) and the fields add up, making a strong, bar-magnet-like field inside. Put in an iron core and you get an electromagnet, the heart of cranes, relays and bells.
Magnetic force on charges and wires

A magnetic field pushes sideways on a moving charge, at right angles to both its motion and the field: Magnetic force F = q v B (charge moving at right angles to B) F = B I L (wire of length L carrying current I) Because the force is sideways, it makes charges move in circles. This bends particle beams in accelerators. The same force on a current-carrying coil makes it turn: that is an electric motor .
Faraday's induction

Michael Faraday asked in 1831: if current makes magnetism, can magnetism make current? Yes, but only when the field is changing . Push a magnet into a coil and a voltage appears. Faraday's law induced voltage = rate of change of magnetic flux (number of turns x B x area) Faster motion, stronger magnet or more turns give more voltage. Joseph Henry in America found the same effect around the same time.
Lenz's law and the generator

Heinrich Lenz showed that the induced current always opposes the change that causes it. This is conservation of energy: if it helped the change, you would get free energy. Push the magnet in and you feel a resistance; that effort is the energy you convert to electricity. A generator spins a coil in a magnetic field, so the flux keeps changing and an alternating voltage appears. The spinning is done by steam, water, wind or diesel. A motor is the reverse: current in, spinning out.
Force on a wire

A wire 0.5 m long carries 2 A in a field of 0.1 tesla at right angles. F = B I L = 0.1 x 2 x 0.5 = 0.1 N . For induction: a coil of 100 turns, with area 0.01 square metres, has flux in a 0.2 T field going from 0.2 x 0.01 x 100 to zero in 0.1 s. Voltage = (0.2 x 0.01 x 100) / 0.1 = 2 V . Spin it faster and the voltage rises.
Magnetism mix-ups

'A steady magnet near a coil makes current.' Only a changing field does. A still magnet does nothing. 'Magnetic force does work on charges.' The force is always sideways to the motion, so it changes direction but not speed. 'Earth's north pole attracts the compass north.' The geographic north is near Earth's magnetic south pole; opposites attract.
Thumba, the magnetic equator and the first rocket

The earth's magnetic equator passes close to Thiruvananthapuram. That is a main reason the Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station was set up there, from where India's first sounding rocket was launched on 21 November 1963. Scientists studied the equatorial electrojet, a current in the upper atmosphere, using such rockets. Nearly all of India's power, from hydro to thermal to wind, comes from generators working on Faraday's law.
Key takeaways

Moving charges create magnetic fields (Oersted, 1820). A field exerts force F = qvB on charges, F = BIL on wires; motors use this. A changing flux induces a voltage (Faraday, 1831); generators use this. Lenz: the induced effect opposes the change. Think about it 1. Why does a magnet dropped through a copper tube fall slowly? 2. A motor can also act as a generator. Why?
Maxwell's Equations and Light as a Wave
The unification that predicted radio

In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell wrote down a few equations that gathered all of electricity and magnetism into one theory. Out of the maths popped a surprise: waves of electric and magnetic fields, travelling at a speed equal to the known speed of light. Maxwell concluded that light itself is an electromagnetic wave. This unlocked radio, television, mobile phones and Wi-Fi.
Four equations, four ideas

Maxwell's equations (1865, refining earlier work) say in words: Gauss's law: electric charges are the source of electric field lines. No monopoles: magnetic field lines never begin or end; they loop. Faraday's law: a changing magnetic field makes an electric field. Ampere-Maxwell law: currents and changing electric fields make magnetic fields. The last fix, Maxwell's addition of the changing electric field term, was the key to waves.
Fields feed each other

Here is the idea. A changing magnetic field produces an electric field (Faraday). A changing electric field produces a magnetic field (Maxwell's addition). So a wiggling field can create a second wiggling field, which creates the first, and the pattern runs off through space by itself. That is an electromagnetic wave : electric and magnetic fields oscillating at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel. It needs no medium. This is how sunlight crosses empty space.
The speed of light drops out

Maxwell's equations contain two constants measured in simple electric and magnetic experiments. Combine them and the wave speed is: Wave speed c = 1 / square root of (mu0 x epsilon0) = 3.0 x 10 to the power 8 m/s This matched the measured speed of light so closely that Maxwell concluded: light is an electromagnetic wave. In vacuum, it travels 300,000 km every second, and the Sun's light reaches us in about 8 minutes 20 seconds.
Hertz and the spectrum

In 1887 Heinrich Hertz generated and detected radio waves in his laboratory, confirming Maxwell. The unit of frequency, the hertz, honours him. Light is only a thin slice of a huge family, the electromagnetic spectrum . From long to short wavelength: radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays. All obey c = f x wavelength; only the frequency differs.
What each band does

Radio: broadcasting, mobile networks. Microwaves: ovens (they shake water molecules), radar, satellite links. Infrared: heat, remote controls, night vision. Visible: what our eyes see, 400 to 700 nanometres. Ultraviolet: sunburn; sterilising. X-rays: pass through flesh; used in medicine. Gamma rays: from nuclei; the most energetic and penetrating.
Radio wavelength

An FM station broadcasts at 100 MHz (100 million hertz). Wavelength = c / f = 3 x 10 to the power 8 / 10 to the power 8 = 3 m . A mobile phone signal at 900 MHz: wavelength = 3 x 10 to the power 8 / 9 x 10 to the power 8 = 0.33 m. Green light of wavelength 550 nm has frequency = 3 x 10 to the power 8 / 5.5 x 10 to the power -7 = 5.5 x 10 to the power 14 Hz, hundreds of trillions of oscillations per second.
Wave myths

'Radio waves and light are different things.' Same kind of wave, just different frequency. 'Microwave ovens are radioactive.' Microwaves are non-ionising radio-type waves; they heat food but do not make it radioactive. 'Light needs air to travel.' Electromagnetic waves travel best in vacuum; sound is the one that needs a medium.
J. C. Bose and the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope

Jagadish Chandra Bose showed millimetre-wavelength radio waves in Calcutta in 1895 and built early solid-state detectors, years before Marconi's first practical radio transmission; he is often honoured as a pioneer of radio and microwave science. Today India's Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (GMRT) near Pune, with 30 dishes, each 45 m across, listens to radio waves from distant galaxies and pulsars. Its design rests on the very same Maxwell's equations.
Key takeaways

Maxwell (1865) unified electricity, magnetism and light. Changing electric and magnetic fields sustain each other as a travelling wave. c = 3 x 10 to the power 8 m/s; c = f x wavelength. The spectrum runs from radio to gamma rays; Hertz confirmed radio waves in 1887. Think about it 1. Why can we see the Sun but not hear it? 2. Why can't your mobile phone get a signal in a lift?
AC, Transformers and the Power Grid
How power travels hundreds of kilometres

A power station in Chhattisgarh lights a bulb in Chennai. The electricity must travel hundreds of kilometres without losing most of its energy on the way. The trick, invented in the 1880s, is to use alternating current and transformers . Behind every wall socket is a continent-scale machine, the grid, tuned to run in perfect rhythm.
DC and AC

Direct current (DC) flows one way, as from a battery. Alternating current (AC) reverses direction many times a second, tracing a sine wave. In India the mains alternates at 50 Hz : 50 complete cycles every second. In the USA it is 60 Hz. AC comes naturally from a generator, a coil turning in a magnetic field. Its great advantage is that a transformer can change AC voltage up or down cheaply. DC cannot do this easily.
RMS: the 'effective' voltage

AC voltage keeps changing, so what does '230 V' mean? It is the root mean square (rms) value, the steady DC voltage that would heat a resistor equally. Peak and rms V(rms) = V(peak) / square root of 2 = 0.707 x V(peak) So 230 V rms mains actually swings up to about 325 V at its peak, then down to -325 V and back, 50 times a second. Appliances are rated by rms values.
The transformer

A transformer has two coils wound on an iron core. AC in the first (primary) coil makes a changing magnetic flux in the core, which induces an AC voltage in the second (secondary) coil. This is Faraday's law at work. Transformer rule V2 / V1 = N2 / N1 (ratio of turns) power in is about power out More turns on the secondary gives a higher voltage and lower current (step-up); fewer turns gives the opposite (step-down). A good transformer is over 98 percent efficient. It works only with AC, since DC gives no changing flux.
Why the grid uses high voltage

Power in a wire is P = V I, and heat lost in the wire is I squared times R. For the same power, raising the voltage ten times cuts the current ten times and the heat loss a hundred times. So power stations step voltage up to hundreds of thousands of volts for long-distance lines, and substations step it down before it reaches your street, then again to 230 V.
The war of the currents and the grid

In the 1880s Thomas Edison backed DC; George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla backed AC. The 'war of the currents' was won by AC because of transformers: only AC could be sent efficiently over long distances. A modern grid links many generators, all spinning in step at exactly 50 Hz in India. If demand rises, the frequency dips; operators must instantly add supply. Keeping this balance is one of the great engineering feats of the age.
Losses on a 100 kW line

Send 100 kW through a line of 1 ohm total resistance. At 230 V: current = 100,000 / 230 = 435 A. Loss = I squared R = 435 squared x 1 = about 189,000 W , more than the power sent. Impossible. At 23,000 V: current = 4.35 A. Loss = 4.35 squared x 1 = 19 W . A loss ten thousand times smaller. Step-down by a transformer with 10,000 turns on the primary to 100 turns: voltage ratio 100, so 23,000 V becomes 230 V.
AC and grid errors

'230 V means the voltage is always 230.' It is an rms value; the instantaneous voltage swings to about 325 V. 'Transformers make power.' They change voltage and current but not total power (apart from small losses). 'A transformer works on a battery.' Only a changing current gives a changing flux; steady DC gives no output.
One Nation, One Grid

India completed its integrated national grid on 31 December 2013, when the Southern Grid was synchronised with the rest.
