Since then power can flow from surplus regions to deficit ones at one frequency, 50 Hz. India's main transmission lines include 400 kV, 765 kV and high-voltage DC links. The Indian grid is now one of the largest synchronised grids in the world, and an increasingly important home to solar and wind power, which makes keeping the frequency steady harder.
Key takeaways

AC alternates; Indian mains is 230 V rms, 50 Hz; peak is about 325 V. Transformers use Faraday's law: V2/V1 = N2/N1; they only work on AC. High-voltage transmission slashes I squared R heat loss. The grid is a synchronised machine, held at one frequency. Think about it 1. If a transformer steps voltage up 10 times, what happens to the current? 2. Why do phone chargers get slightly warm?
Reflection, Refraction and Lenses
From spectacles to the internet

Light bends, bounces and focuses, and these simple facts built spectacles, microscopes, telescopes, cameras and the glass-fibre cables that carry the internet under the sea. All you need to describe most of it is the idea of a ray , a straight line along which light travels. This is geometric optics .
Reflection

When light hits a smooth surface, it bounces. The law of reflection : the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal (the line at right angles to the surface). A plane mirror gives a virtual image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, the same size, left and right swapped. A rough surface scatters light in all directions, which is why we can see paper from every angle but not ourselves in it.
Refraction and Snell's law

When light passes from one material into another, it changes speed and bends. In glass it travels about 1.5 times slower than in vacuum. Snell's law n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2) The refractive index n is c divided by the speed in the material: water 1.33, glass about 1.5, diamond 2.42. Light bends toward the normal on entering a denser material. This is why a straw looks bent in water and a swimming pool looks shallower than it is. Willebrord Snell found the law in 1621.
Total internal reflection

Going from dense to less dense material (glass to air), light bends away from the normal. Increase the angle and it eventually skims along the surface. Beyond this critical angle , all light reflects back inside: Critical angle sin(theta c) = n2 / n1 For glass (1.5) to air (1), sin(theta c) = 0.667, so theta c is about 42 degrees. This makes diamonds sparkle and powers optical fibres : light zigzags down a glass thread, trapped, carrying data across oceans. Charles Kao's 1966 work on low-loss fibre won the Nobel Prize in 2009.
Lenses

A convex (converging) lens is thicker in the middle and brings parallel rays to a focus at distance f, the focal length. A concave lens spreads them out. Lenses work by refraction at curved surfaces. Lens formula 1/v - 1/u = 1/f (with u negative for an object on the left) magnification m = v / u power P = 1/f in dioptres (f in metres)
The eye and optical instruments

Your eye is a lens system: the cornea and lens focus an upside-down image on the retina. Short-sighted people focus in front of the retina; a concave lens fixes it. Long-sighted people focus behind it; a convex lens helps. Doctors prescribe lens power in dioptres. A microscope uses two convex lenses to magnify tiny things. A telescope gathers faint light with a big lens or mirror. Galileo pointed one at the sky in 1609 and saw Jupiter's moons.
Where does the image form?

An object is 30 cm from a convex lens of f = 10 cm. Using u = -30 and f = +10: 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/10 - 1/30 = 2/30, so v = +15 cm . Magnification m = v/u = 15 / (-30) = -0.5 . The image is real, inverted and half the size (see diagram). Spectacle power: a lens of f = 50 cm = 0.5 m has power 1/0.5 = +2 dioptres.
Light misreadings

'The straw really bends in water.' The light bends; the straw is straight. 'Covering half a lens shows half the image.' You still see the whole image, only dimmer. 'Light speeds up in glass.' It slows down in any material compared with vacuum.
Raman's blue sea and BharatNet

In 1921, sailing home from England, C. V. Raman looked at the deep blue of the Mediterranean and doubted the textbook answer that it just reflects the sky. Back in Calcutta he worked out that water molecules themselves scatter blue light more than red. That curiosity led to the Raman effect, on which he won the Nobel Prize in 1930. India's BharatNet project lays optical fibre to connect gram panchayats across the country, using total internal reflection to carry broadband to villages.
Key takeaways

Reflection: angle in equals angle out. Refraction: n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2); n = c / speed in medium. Total internal reflection beyond the critical angle powers optical fibre. Lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f; power = 1/f in dioptres. Think about it 1. Why does a pool look shallower than it really is? 2. Why do diamonds sparkle more than glass?
Interference, Diffraction and Polarisation
The evidence that light is a wave

Is light a stream of tiny particles, as Newton believed, or a wave? Newton's followers dominated for a century. In 1801 Thomas Young settled the matter with a simple experiment: he made light interfere. Interference, diffraction and polarisation are behaviours that only waves show. They explain soap-bubble colours, the rainbow sheen of a CD, and how sunglasses cut glare.
Waves of light add up

Recall that when two waves meet, they add. If the crest of one meets the crest of another ( in phase ) they reinforce: constructive interference , bright. If crest meets trough ( out of phase ) they cancel: destructive interference , dark. Whether waves meet in phase depends on the difference in the path each travelled. A path difference of a whole number of wavelengths gives brightness; a half-wavelength extra gives darkness.
Young's double-slit experiment

Shine light through two very narrow slits close together. On a screen beyond, you see alternating bright and dark stripes, called fringes . Particles would give two plain bands; only waves can make stripes. Fringe spacing spacing = (wavelength x D) / d D is the slit-to-screen distance and d the slit separation. Red light (longer wavelength) gives wider fringes than blue. Young used this in 1801 to measure wavelengths of light, which are a few hundred nanometres.
Diffraction: waves bend round corners

Waves spread when they pass an opening or edge. Sound turns a corner so you hear someone round a wall; light also spreads, but its wavelength is so tiny that the effect is visible only for very small openings. Light through a single narrow slit makes a wide central bright band with fainter bands on either side. A diffraction grating , thousands of slits per centimetre, splits light into sharp colours and is the heart of spectrometers. The rainbow sheen of a CD is a grating effect.
Thin films and soap bubbles

Light reflecting from the front and back of a very thin film (soap, oil on water) interferes. Where the film's thickness makes certain colours reinforce, you see bright colour. As the film thins and the thickness changes, the colours swirl. Anti-reflection coatings on camera lenses and spectacles use this deliberately: a layer of the right thickness cancels reflected light, letting more through.
Polarisation

Light is a transverse wave, so its electric field vibrates at right angles to its direction. Ordinary light vibrates in all such directions. A polarising filter lets through only one direction. Light reflected off water or a road is partly polarised horizontally. Polaroid sunglasses block that direction, cutting glare. Polarisation cannot happen with sound in air, because sound is longitudinal. Etienne Malus found polarisation by reflection in 1808. LCD screens use polarisers too.
Fringe spacing

Light of wavelength 600 nm (6 x 10 to the power -7 m) passes through slits 0.5 mm apart onto a screen 1 m away. Spacing = 6 x 10 to the power -7 x 1 / (5 x 10 to the power -4) = 1.2 x 10 to the power -3 m = 1.2 mm . Use blue light of 450 nm instead and the spacing falls to 0.9 mm. Fringes are tiny, which is why we do not see interference in everyday light.
Misreadings

'Interference destroys energy.' The energy missing in dark fringes appears in the bright ones; the total is conserved. 'Light never bends round corners.' It does, but only a little because its wavelength is tiny. 'Polarised light is a different kind of light.' It is the same light with the vibration restricted to one direction.
Raman, Bose and polarised waves

On 28 February 1928 C. V. Raman and K. S. Krishnan observed that when light scatters from molecules, a small part comes out with shifted colour, because the light has swapped energy with the molecules. The Raman effect won the Nobel Prize in 1930, the first for an Asian in science. India celebrates 28 February as National Science Day. J. C. Bose in the 1890s used polarisers and prisms with microwaves, showing that radio waves polarise just like light.
Key takeaways

Interference: waves add, giving bright and dark fringes (Young, 1801). Fringe spacing = wavelength x D / d. Diffraction: waves spread around small obstacles and slits. Polarisation shows light is a transverse wave; Polaroid filters cut glare. Think about it 1. Why do soap bubbles show changing colours? 2. Why can you hear around a corner but not see around it?
Special Relativity
Time is not what it seems

In 1905, a 26-year-old patent clerk in Bern published a paper that changed how we think about space and time. Albert Einstein showed that time can run at different rates for different observers, and that mass and energy are two faces of the same thing. This is not just theory: it is built into your phone's GPS, into particle accelerators and into nuclear power.
The puzzle of light

Maxwell's equations gave the speed of light as a fixed number. But relative to what? People imagined an invisible medium, the 'ether'. In 1887 Michelson and Morley tried to detect Earth's motion through it and found nothing. Einstein took the result at face value. His two postulates (1905): 1. The laws of physics are the same for all observers moving at steady speed. 2. The speed of light in vacuum, c = 300,000 km/s, is the same for all such observers, whatever the motion of the source or the observer.
Time dilation

If light's speed is the same for everyone, then something else must give: time. Moving clocks run slow. Time dilation t(moving observer sees) = gamma x t0 gamma = 1 / square root of (1 - v squared / c squared) At everyday speeds gamma is 1 to a hundred decimal places, so we never notice. Near light speed it grows without limit.
Length contraction and simultaneity

Along the direction of motion, moving objects measure shorter: L = L0 / gamma. A rocket at 0.6c is seen only 80 percent as long. Even 'at the same time' is relative. Two events simultaneous for one observer may not be for another moving past. Nothing is wrong: we simply must give up a single universal clock. Space and time merge into one four-dimensional spacetime , as Hermann Minkowski showed in 1908.
E = mc squared

Einstein's best-known result: Mass-energy E = m c squared Mass is concentrated energy. Since c squared is huge (9 x 10 to the power 16), a tiny mass holds a vast energy. One gram of matter equals 9 x 10 to the power 13 joules, about the energy of a 20-kiloton bomb. In nuclear reactions and in the Sun, a little mass is turned into energy. Nothing with mass can reach light speed, since its energy would become infinite.
Proof in the real world

Muons: these particles made in the upper atmosphere live only 2.2 microseconds, enough to travel 660 m, yet they reach the ground, thanks to time dilation. GPS: satellite clocks run fast by about 45 microseconds a day because of weaker gravity and slow by 7 because of their speed. Without correction for both effects, positions would drift by kilometres each day. Accelerators: particles reach 99.9999 percent of light speed and gain mass-energy, as predicted.
A fast space traveller

A spacecraft moves at v = 0.6c. gamma = 1 / square root of (1 - 0.36) = 1 / 0.8 = 1.25 . A journey that takes 4 years on the ship's clock takes 4 x 1.25 = 5 years by Earth clocks. At 0.9c, gamma = 2.29: the traveller ages only 4 years while Earth ages 9.2. At 0.99c, gamma is about 7.
Relativity myths

'Relativity says everything is relative.' It says the speed of light and the laws of physics are the same for all; what changes are time and length. 'Moving objects really get heavier.' Better to say their energy and momentum grow; modern texts keep mass fixed. 'You can outrun light with enough fuel.' It would need infinite energy.
Bose, Einstein and NavIC

In 1924 Satyendra Nath Bose sent Einstein a paper on light quanta; Einstein translated it into German and got it published. Their joint work gave us Bose-Einstein statistics. India's own satellite navigation system, NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation), must correct its clocks for relativistic effects, just like GPS, to give position accurate to a few metres.
Key takeaways

Postulates: same physics for all steady observers; c is the same for all. Moving clocks run slow by gamma = 1 / root(1 - v squared / c squared). Moving lengths contract along the motion; nothing with mass reaches c. E = mc squared: mass is stored energy. Think about it 1. Why do we never notice time dilation in daily life? 2. How does time dilation let muons reach Earth's surface?
General Relativity
Gravity is not a force at all

Newton described how gravity acts but not what it is. Einstein asked why gravity seems to pull all things equally, and found an answer so strange that it took four years of hard work: gravity is the curvature of spacetime . His general theory of relativity (1915) predicts black holes, gravitational waves and the expanding universe. It has passed every test for over a century.
The equivalence principle

Einstein's 'happiest thought' (1907): a person in free fall feels no weight. Inside a closed lift, you cannot tell whether you are at rest on Earth's surface or being accelerated upward in empty space; both feel the same. This equivalence principle says gravity and acceleration are indistinguishable. It explains why all objects fall at the same rate: they are simply following the same natural path.
Curved spacetime

In general relativity, mass and energy bend the fabric of spacetime. Free objects follow the straightest possible paths in that curved geometry. To us, the paths look curved, and we call it gravity. John Wheeler's summary: spacetime tells matter how to move; matter tells spacetime how to curve. The rubber-sheet picture is an analogy: a heavy ball dents the sheet and a small ball rolls toward it.
Tests that came true

Mercury's orbit (1915): Newton could not explain a slow turning of Mercury's orbit by 43 arc-seconds per century. Einstein's theory gave exactly 43. Bending of starlight (1919): Arthur Eddington's solar eclipse expeditions saw stars near the Sun shifted, as predicted, making Einstein world famous. Gravitational redshift and time: clocks run slower deeper in gravity; GPS must correct for it.
Black holes

If enough mass is squeezed into a small region, spacetime curves so steeply that nothing, not even light, escapes. The boundary is the event horizon . Its size for mass M is the Schwarzschild radius, found by Karl Schwarzschild in 1916: Schwarzschild radius r = 2 G M / c squared For the Sun it is about 3 km; for Earth, about 9 mm. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of a black hole's shadow, in galaxy M87; in 2022 came the one at our Milky Way's centre.
Gravitational waves

Accelerating masses send ripples through spacetime at the speed of light. Einstein predicted them in 1916 but doubted they could be detected. On 14 September 2015 the LIGO detectors in the USA caught the ripples from two black holes merging over a billion years ago. The announcement came in February 2016 and the Nobel Prize followed in 2017. The distance change measured was smaller than one-thousandth the width of a proton.
How small is the Earth as a black hole?

r = 2 G M / c squared with G = 6.67 x 10 to the power -11, M = 6 x 10 to the power 24 kg, c = 3 x 10 to the power 8. r = 2 x 6.67e-11 x 6e24 / 9e16 = 8.0e14 / 9e16 = about 0.009 m , nine millimetres. To become a black hole, Earth would have to be crushed to the size of a marble. The Sun's radius (700,000 km) is far larger than its 3 km Schwarzschild radius, so it is no black hole.
Misreadings of gravity

'Black holes suck everything in.' At a distance, a black hole's gravity is the same as any star of the same mass. Our Sun swapped for a black hole of equal mass would leave Earth's orbit unchanged. 'Relativity replaced Newton.' It extends it. Newton's law is an excellent approximation for weak gravity and slow speeds. 'The rubber sheet is the real thing.' It is only a 2D picture of 4D spacetime.
Chandrasekhar and LIGO-India

In 1930, aged 19, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar sailed from India to England and worked out that a dying star heavier than about 1.4 Suns cannot settle into a white dwarf and must collapse further. This Chandrasekhar limit points to neutron stars and black holes. He won the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics. India is building LIGO-India , a gravitational-wave detector in Hingoli, Maharashtra, approved in 2016. Jayant Narlikar and the institute IUCAA in Pune have long led Indian research on gravity and cosmology.
Key takeaways

Equivalence principle: gravity and acceleration are locally indistinguishable. Mass-energy curves spacetime; objects follow straight paths in it. Tests: Mercury (43 arc-seconds per century), 1919 eclipse, GPS, black-hole images, gravitational waves. Schwarzschild radius r = 2GM / c squared. Think about it 1. Why do a hammer and a feather fall together in a vacuum, in terms of spacetime? 2. Why do GPS satellite clocks need relativity corrections?
The Photon and the Atom
The theory that broke Newton's world

Around 1900, classical physics could not explain why a hot poker glows the colours it does, why atoms do not collapse, or why shining light on metal knocks out electrons. The fix needed a radical idea: energy comes in tiny packets, called quanta . This idea started quantum mechanics, the theory behind chemistry, lasers, computers and the chips in your phone.
Planck's quantum (1900)

Hot objects glow with a spectrum that classical physics could not explain. Max Planck found in 1900 that the curve fits if light is emitted in lumps of energy: Planck's relation E = h x f f is the frequency and h is Planck's constant , 6.63 x 10 to the power -34 joule second. Higher frequency, bigger lump. Planck thought it a mathematical trick; it was the first hint of a new physics.
Einstein and the photoelectric effect

Shine light on a metal and electrons can be knocked out. Surprises: below a certain frequency no electrons come out, however bright the light. Above it, they come at once, and brighter light gives more electrons, not faster ones. Einstein explained in 1905: light itself is made of particles, photons , each with energy hf. One photon knocks out one electron: Photoelectric equation kinetic energy of electron = h f - (work function) He won the 1921 Nobel Prize for this, not for relativity.
The Bohr atom

Rutherford's atom (1911) has electrons orbiting a tiny nucleus, but classical physics said they should spiral in and crash. In 1913 Niels Bohr proposed that electrons can occupy only certain energy levels and radiate only when jumping between them. For hydrogen: E(n) = -13.6 eV divided by n squared. A jump emits a photon with energy equal to the gap, giving the sharp coloured lines of atomic spectra. Every element has its own fingerprint, so we can read the chemistry of distant stars.
Matter waves

If light waves can act like particles, perhaps particles act like waves. Louis de Broglie suggested in 1924: de Broglie wavelength wavelength = h / (m v) For an electron the wavelength is tiny but real, and electrons were seen to diffract in 1927. This is wave-particle duality . Electron microscopes use electron waves to see far smaller details than light can.
Uncertainty and the quantum rules

Werner Heisenberg (1927) showed we cannot know both position and momentum precisely at the same time: the product of their uncertainties is at least about h divided by 4 pi. It is not about clumsy instruments; it is built into nature. Erwin Schrodinger's equation (1926) describes electrons by a wave function whose square gives the probability of finding the particle somewhere. Quantum physics predicts chances, not certainties.
Energy of a photon and photoelectric emission

A handy rule: E (in eV) = 1240 / wavelength (in nm). For green light of 550 nm, E = 1240 / 550 = 2.25 eV . Sodium has a work function of about 2.3 eV. Red light at 700 nm has 1.77 eV: no electrons , however bright. Blue light at 400 nm has 3.1 eV, so electrons emerge with energy 3.1 - 2.3 = 0.8 eV . Hydrogen jump n = 3 to 2: 3.4 - 1.5 = 1.9 eV, wavelength 1240 / 1.9 = 650 nm, the red line.
Quantum myths

'Electrons orbit like tiny planets.' Bohr's picture is a useful stepping stone; real electrons are spread-out clouds of probability. 'Brighter light always gives faster photoelectrons.' Brightness gives more electrons; only higher frequency gives faster ones. 'Uncertainty is about measuring badly.' It is a basic property of nature.
Bose, Raman and Saha

S. N. Bose's 1924 work, treating photons as indistinguishable particles, gave the correct counting for light quanta and launched Bose-Einstein statistics. Particles that follow it, such as photons and the Higgs, are called bosons in his honour. C. V. Raman's 1928 effect is a direct sign of the photon: a photon loses or gains a bit of energy when it hits a molecule, appearing at a shifted colour. Meghnad Saha's 1920 equation links atomic energy levels to the temperature of stars.
Key takeaways

Energy comes in quanta: E = hf (Planck 1900). Photons explain the photoelectric effect (Einstein 1905). Atoms have discrete levels; jumps produce spectral lines (Bohr 1913). Matter has a wavelength h/mv; the uncertainty principle limits what we can know. Think about it 1. Why can a dim blue light eject electrons while a bright red light cannot? 2. Why does each element have its own line spectrum?
Nuclear Physics: Fission and Fusion
A tiny core with enormous power

The Sun shines, nuclear reactors light cities, doctors treat cancer with radiation, and archaeologists date bones, all because of the atomic nucleus. It is about 100,000 times smaller than the atom, yet holds almost all its mass and a vast store of energy. Nuclear physics also brought the atom bomb. Understanding it is part of understanding the modern world.
Inside the nucleus

Ernest Rutherford showed in 1911 that an atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus. It holds protons (positive) and neutrons (neutral, found by James Chadwick in 1932), together called nucleons. The number of protons Z fixes the element; protons plus neutrons is the mass number A. Isotopes have the same Z but different neutron counts: carbon-12 and carbon-14 are both carbon. The strong nuclear force glues nucleons together against the protons' electric repulsion, acting only over about a femtometre.
Binding energy and E = mc squared

A nucleus weighs a little less than its separate protons and neutrons. The missing mass became the energy that binds it, by E = mc squared. Per nucleon, binding energy rises up to iron (A about 56) and then falls slowly. That curve explains everything. Splitting very heavy nuclei ( fission ) or joining very light ones ( fusion ) moves toward iron and releases energy.
Radioactivity and half-life

Henri Becquerel found radioactivity in 1896; Marie and Pierre Curie isolated polonium and radium soon after. Unstable nuclei decay on their own, emitting alpha particles (helium nuclei), beta particles (electrons) or gamma rays. Each decay is random, but a large sample has a steady half-life : the time for half to decay. N = N0 x (1/2) to the power (t / half-life). Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years, so measuring it in old bone gives its age. Medical isotopes decay in hours or days.
Nuclear fission

In 1938-39 Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann split uranium, and Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained it. A slow neutron hits uranium-235, which splits into two lighter nuclei, 2 or 3 neutrons and about 200 MeV of energy. The neutrons can split more nuclei: a chain reaction . Enrico Fermi achieved the first controlled one in Chicago in 1942. In a reactor, control rods absorb neutrons to keep it steady; in a bomb it runs away. One kilogram of U-235 releases about 8 x 10 to the power 13 joules, millions of times more than a kilogram of coal.
Nuclear fusion

Fusion joins light nuclei. In the Sun's core at about 15 million kelvin, four hydrogen nuclei fuse into one helium nucleus, turning about 0.7 percent of their mass into energy. The Sun converts around 4 million tonnes of mass to light every second. Nuclei repel, so fusion needs huge temperature and pressure. On Earth, experiments such as ITER in France aim to make fusion power from hydrogen isotopes. It promises abundant fuel and little long-lived waste, but a net-power plant remains a work in progress.
Half-life arithmetic

A sample of 80 g of an isotope with a half-life of 8 days. After 24 days that is 3 half-lives: 80 to 40 to 20 to 10 g . Energy from mass: a nuclear reaction that loses 0.1 g of mass releases E = 0.0001 x (3 x 10 to the power 8) squared = 9 x 10 to the power 12 J . Check against fission: 200 MeV per U-235 nucleus is about 3.2 x 10 to the power -11 J; one kilogram has roughly 2.6 x 10 to the power 24 nuclei, giving about 8 x 10 to the power 13 J.
Nuclear myths

'A nuclear reactor can explode like a bomb.' Reactor fuel is not concentrated enough, and the design cannot detonate; accidents involve overheating, not a bomb blast. 'After one half-life, then another half-life, everything is gone.' Half the remainder decays each time; it never reaches exactly zero. 'Radiation is always man-made.' Natural background radiation comes from rocks, space and even bananas (potassium-40).
Bhabha's three stages

Homi J. Bhabha founded the Atomic Energy Establishment at Trombay, now named after him. In the 1950s he set out India's three-stage nuclear programme : natural uranium reactors, then fast breeder reactors using plutonium, then reactors burning India's large thorium reserves with uranium-233. The Apsara research reactor at Trombay began running in August 1956, Asia's first research reactor. Today plants such as Kudankulam in Tamil Nadu supply power, and India has tested nuclear devices in 1974 and 1998.
Key takeaways

The nucleus holds protons and neutrons bound by the strong force. Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron: fission of heavy and fusion of light nuclei release energy. Radioactive decay follows half-life: N = N0 x (1/2) to the power (t/T). Fission powers reactors; fusion powers the Sun. Think about it 1. Why can iron not release energy by either fission or fusion? 2. Why does fusion require such high temperature?
Particle Physics and the Standard Model
What is everything made of?

Ancient Indian and Greek thinkers imagined indivisible atoms. We now know atoms split into protons, neutrons and electrons, and the protons and neutrons themselves split into quarks. The question 'what are the smallest building blocks and how do they interact?' is the aim of particle physics. Its answer is the Standard Model , one of the most precisely tested theories in all of science.
The four forces

Everything that happens in the universe comes from four forces: Gravity: weakest, but acts across space and adds up for big masses. Electromagnetism: between charged particles; holds atoms together. Strong nuclear force: binds quarks into protons and neutrons, and nucleons into nuclei. Weak nuclear force: causes certain radioactive decays and powers the Sun's fusion. The Standard Model describes the last three. Gravity is not yet included.
Quarks and leptons

Matter particles come in two families. Quarks feel the strong force and come in six types: up, down, charm, strange, top, bottom. Leptons do not: the electron, muon, tau, and three nearly massless neutrinos . Ordinary matter needs only up quarks, down quarks and electrons. A proton is two ups and one down (uud); a neutron is up, down, down (udd). The heavier families appear in cosmic rays and accelerators and decay quickly. Quarks are never seen alone.
Force carriers

In quantum field theory, forces arise when particles exchange other particles. Electromagnetism is carried by the photon ; the strong force by gluons ; the weak force by the heavy W and Z bosons. Richard Feynman drew diagrams to show these exchanges. Quantum electrodynamics, the theory of light and electrons, predicts the electron's magnetic strength correct to about ten decimal places, the most accurate prediction in science.
Antimatter

Paul Dirac predicted in 1928 that every particle has an antiparticle with the same mass and opposite charge. Carl Anderson found the positron, the anti-electron, in 1932. When a particle meets its antiparticle they annihilate into energy (E = mc squared). Hospitals use PET scanners, where positrons from a tracer annihilate with electrons and give off gamma rays that form an image. Why the universe has more matter than antimatter remains unexplained.
The Higgs boson

The Standard Model's equations at first required massless particles. In 1964, Peter Higgs, Francois Englert and others proposed a field filling all space which gives particles mass by interacting with them; the Higgs boson is its ripple. On 4 July 2012 the ATLAS and CMS experiments at CERN's Large Hadron Collider announced the discovery, at a mass of about 125 times the proton's. Higgs and Englert shared the 2013 Nobel Prize. The LHC, a 27 km ring near Geneva, collides protons at the energy of 13.6 trillion electron volts.
Adding charges and annihilation

Proton (uud): +2/3 + 2/3 - 1/3 = +1 . Neutron (udd): +2/3 - 1/3 - 1/3 = 0 . Electron-positron annihilation: each has rest mass energy 0.511 MeV, so two gamma photons carry a total of 2 x 0.511 = 1.022 MeV , each 0.511 MeV. Photon wavelength = 1240 eV nm / 511,000 eV = 0.0024 nm, a very short-wavelength gamma ray.
Particle myths

'The Higgs boson is the God particle.' A nickname the physicists mostly dislike; it explains mass for some particles, not everything. 'Most of your mass is the Higgs.' Most of a proton's mass comes from the strong force's energy, not from the quark masses. 'Antimatter is science fiction.' It is made routinely in labs and used in PET scans.
Bose, Bhabha and CERN

The word boson honours S. N. Bose, so the Higgs boson carries an Indian name. Homi Bhabha worked out in 1935 how electrons scatter off positrons, now called Bhabha scattering, a process studied at every electron-positron collider. Indian scientists contribute to experiments at the LHC, including CMS and ALICE, and India became an Associate Member of CERN in January 2017. The India-based Neutrino Observatory was planned in Tamil Nadu to study atmospheric neutrinos, though it awaits final go-ahead.
Key takeaways

Four forces: gravity, electromagnetic, strong, weak. Matter: six quarks and six leptons; proton = uud, neutron = udd. Forces are carried by photons, gluons, W and Z; the Higgs field gives mass (Higgs discovered 2012). Every particle has an antiparticle; annihilation turns mass into energy. Think about it 1. Why are quarks never seen alone? 2. Why does a PET scan use antimatter?
Semiconductors and Modern Technology
The material that runs the modern world

Your phone holds billions of tiny switches, each smaller than a virus. Every computer, camera, solar panel and LED depends on a few special materials called semiconductors , mostly silicon. They sit between conductors and insulators, and their great trick is that you can control how well they conduct. That control lets us build electronic switches and amplifiers.
Bands and conductivity

In a solid, electron energies group into bands with gaps. In a metal the top band is partly full, so electrons move freely. In an insulator the gap above the full band is huge, so nothing moves. In a semiconductor the gap is small (silicon: 1.1 eV), so heat or light can lift a few electrons across. An electron that leaves a vacancy, a 'hole', lets neighbours hop in; the hole acts like a positive charge. Unlike metals, semiconductors conduct better when warmed.
Doping: n-type and p-type

Pure silicon conducts poorly. Adding tiny impurities, doping , changes that. Add phosphorus (5 outer electrons) and you get spare electrons: n-type . Add boron (3 outer electrons) and you get holes: p-type . One impurity atom per million silicon atoms can change conductivity by a factor of thousands. Doping gives engineers a dial.
The p-n junction diode

Join p-type and n-type and electrons and holes meet at the junction, forming a thin zone with no free carriers, and a built-in voltage (about 0.7 V in silicon). Connect a battery one way (forward bias) and current flows; the other way (reverse bias) almost none. This one-way valve is a diode , used to turn AC into DC. A light-emitting diode (LED) gives out light when electrons fall across the gap; a solar cell works in reverse, light making current.
The transistor

John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley at Bell Labs made the first transistor in December 1947, and shared the 1956 Nobel Prize. A transistor uses a small voltage or current at one terminal to control a large current between the other two, so it works as an amplifier or a fast on-off switch. Switches make logic: combinations of transistors add numbers and store bits. Every digital device is a vast network of them.
Integrated circuits and Moore's law

Jack Kilby (1958) and Robert Noyce (1959) put many transistors on a single chip, the integrated circuit . In 1965 Gordon Moore noticed that the number on a chip doubled roughly every two years, a trend called Moore's law . From a few thousand transistors in the 1970s, chips now hold tens of billions. Progress has slowed as features approach a few nanometres, near the size of atoms.
Lasers and other quantum devices

Lasers (Theodore Maiman, 1960) use quantum jumps to make light of one colour, travelling in step. Semiconductor lasers read barcodes and send internet data down optical fibre. The blue LED, by Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura (Nobel 2014), made efficient white LED lighting possible. MRI scanners rely on superconducting magnets and nuclear spin. All of these rest on quantum physics.
Choosing a resistor for an LED

A red LED needs about 2 V and 20 mA. Run it from a 5 V supply. The resistor must drop the remaining 3 V. R = V / I = 3 / 0.02 = 150 ohms . Power in the resistor = 3 x 0.02 = 0.06 W, so a small resistor will do. Moore's law check: 2,300 transistors in the Intel 4004 (1971) doubling every 2 years for 50 years gives 2,300 x 2 to the power 25, which is about 77 billion, close to the largest chips today.
Chip misunderstandings

'Semiconductors are just poor conductors.' Their value is that conduction is controllable. 'Doped silicon is electrically charged.' It is neutral; the impurity atoms bring along their own balancing charge. 'Computers think with electricity flowing in wires like water.' Signals are voltage changes switching transistors on and off.
From Bose's crystal to the India Semiconductor Mission

Jagadish Chandra Bose used a crystal of galena, a natural semiconductor, to detect radio waves around 1900, and obtained a US patent in 1904 for a semiconductor detector. This is among the earliest uses of a semiconductor device. India launched the India Semiconductor Mission in 2021 to build chip fabrication and packaging plants. India already supplies a large share of the world's chip design engineers, with major design centres in Bengaluru and Hyderabad.
Key takeaways

Semiconductors have a small band gap; doping makes n-type (electrons) or p-type (holes). A p-n junction is a diode: current one way. LEDs and solar cells are junctions. The transistor (1947) is an electrically controlled switch; chips hold billions. Moore's law: transistor numbers doubled about every two years. Think about it 1. Why does a semiconductor conduct better when heated, unlike a metal? 2. How can a solar cell be seen as an LED running backwards?
Open Questions in Physics
Physics is far from finished

It is tempting to think everything is settled. In truth, our best theories describe only about 5 percent of what the universe contains. The rest is dark and unexplained. And the two pillars of modern physics, quantum theory and general relativity, do not fit together. This lesson is a tour of the frontier: where today's questions are, and what a curious learner can watch for.
The expanding universe

Georges Lemaitre (1927) and Edwin Hubble (1929) showed distant galaxies recede, and the farther, the faster: v = H0 x d , where H0 is about 70 km/s per megaparsec. Space itself is expanding. Run it backwards and everything was once hot and dense. This is the Big Bang , about 13.8 billion years ago. Its afterglow, the cosmic microwave background at 2.7 kelvin, was found by Penzias and Wilson in 1965.
Dark matter

Stars at the edges of galaxies orbit far too fast for the gravity of visible matter. Vera Rubin's measurements in the 1970s showed this. Something unseen, dark matter , adds about five times as much mass as ordinary matter. It also bends light from distant galaxies. It does not glow or absorb light. Experiments deep underground hunt for its particles, so far without success. Whether it is a new particle, or our gravity needs changing, is open.
Dark energy

In 1998, two teams measuring distant exploding stars found that the expansion of the universe is speeding up , a discovery that earned the 2011 Nobel Prize. Something, called dark energy , seems to push space apart. It makes up about 68 percent of the total (as measured by the Planck satellite). The simplest idea is the energy of empty space itself, but a naive quantum calculation overshoots the observed value by a huge factor, perhaps the worst prediction in physics.
Why is there something rather than nothing?

The Big Bang should have made equal matter and antimatter, which would annihilate into light. Yet the universe is made of matter. A tiny excess, about one part in a billion, survived. Why? Known physics cannot explain it. Related puzzles: why do neutrinos have mass (confirmed by 1998 experiments, not in the original Standard Model)? And why are the constants of nature what they are, so finely tuned that stars and life can exist?
Quantum gravity and tensions

Inside a black hole or at the Big Bang, gravity and quantum effects both matter, and our two theories clash. Candidates for a joint theory include string theory and loop quantum gravity , but neither has been tested. Other open questions: the Hubble tension , where the expansion rate measured from the early universe (about 67 km/s per Mpc) disagrees with nearby measurements (about 73), and what 'measurement' means in quantum theory. These are unsettled as of 2026.
Using Hubble's law

A galaxy is 100 megaparsecs away (about 326 million light-years). Its recession speed: v = 70 x 100 = 7000 km/s . Age estimate: 1 / H0. With H0 = 70 km/s per Mpc and 1 Mpc = 3.09 x 10 to the power 19 km, 1/H0 = 3.09e19 / 70 = 4.4e17 s = about 14 billion years , close to the true age of 13.8 billion. The Hubble tension: using 67 instead of 73 changes the answer, and nobody yet knows why the values differ.
Cosmic confusion

'The Big Bang was an explosion in space.' It was the expansion of space itself, everywhere at once; there is no centre. 'Dark matter is just dark gas.' Ordinary dark gas and dust are too little and would be seen in other ways. 'Scientists don't know anything about the universe.' The standard model of cosmology fits a vast amount of precise data; the unknowns lie in particular components.
Raychaudhuri, Narlikar and Aditya-L1

Amal Kumar Raychaudhuri's equation (1955) shows how matter focuses under gravity and became a basis of Penrose and Hawking's singularity theorems about black holes and the Big Bang. Jayant Narlikar, with Fred Hoyle, explored alternatives to the Big Bang and founded IUCAA in Pune. India's space telescope AstroSat launched in 2015, and the Aditya-L1 solar mission, launched on 2 September 2023, studies our Sun from a gravitational balance point. LIGO-India and the GMRT will keep adding to cosmic data.
Key takeaways

The universe is expanding (v = H0 d) from a hot Big Bang 13.8 billion years ago. About 5 percent ordinary matter, 27 percent dark matter, 68 percent dark energy. Open problems: matter-antimatter imbalance, quantum gravity, neutrino mass, the Hubble tension. Science advances by finding where theories fail. Think about it 1. How could we tell dark matter from changed gravity? 2. Why does a discrepancy like the Hubble tension excite scientists rather than worry them?
